cards.title: A small-town tinkerer
cards.body: Claude Shannon was born in 1916 and grew up in Gaylord, a small town in northern Michigan. He built model planes and a radio-controlled boat, and fixed the town's broken radios. His hero was Thomas Edison, who later turned out to be a distant relative.

cards.title: A fence telegraph
cards.body: As a boy he turned a half-mile stretch of barbed-wire fence into a private telegraph line to a friend's house, powered by batteries, with a key at each end for tapping coded messages. His favorite story was Poe's "The Gold-Bug", which ends with someone cracking a secret cipher.

cards.title: College years
bullets: 1932: starts at the University of Michigan.
Earns two degrees at once: mathematics and electrical engineering.
1936: answers a postcard asking for a helper on a big calculating machine at MIT.

cards.title: Bush's room-sized brain
cards.body: At MIT he helped run Vannevar Bush's differential analyzer: a room-sized analog computer whose spinning shafts, gears and wheels acted out an equation. A box of about 100 relays controlled it, and that box got Shannon thinking about switches.

cards.title: Boole's algebra
cards.body: In the 1800s George Boole wrote logic as algebra: true is 1, false is 0, and statements combine with AND, OR and NOT. Shannon first met it in a philosophy class at Michigan, where it was taught as a curiosity with no practical use.

cards.title: Switches do logic
bullets: Closed switch = 1, open switch = 0.
Series: current flows only if both are closed. That is AND.
Parallel: current flows if either one, or both, is closed. That is OR, so 1 + 1 = 1.
A contact that opens when its relay fires acts as NOT.

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
def series(a, b):    # AND
    return a and b

def parallel(a, b):  # OR
    return a or b

print(series(1, 0))    # 0
print(parallel(1, 0))  # 1
print(parallel(1, 1))  # 1

cards.title: Simplify on paper
cards.body: Since a circuit is now an equation, you can shrink it with algebra before touching a wire. Example: y·z + y·z' = y·(z + z'). A switch is either closed or open, so z + z' is always 1, and the whole thing is just y: one switch does the work of four contacts. Also handy: y·y = y and y + y = y.

cards.title: The 1937 thesis
cards.body: Shannon finished his master's thesis, "A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits", in fall 1937 at age 21; it was published the next year and won the Alfred Noble Prize. It turned circuit design from guesswork into a science, and every digital computer's logic gates follow the same idea.

cards.title: Into Bell Labs
bullets: 1940: MIT master's and PhD together; the PhD applied algebra to genetics.
A year at the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton.
Wartime: full-time research mathematician at Bell Labs.
Checked the math for SIGSALY, a secret phone scrambler, without being told what it was for.

cards.title: The one-time pad
cards.body: A one-time pad hides a message with a key of truly random symbols that is as long as the message, kept secret, and used only once. In a classified 1945 report, "A Mathematical Theory of Cryptography", Shannon gave the first proof that such a cipher cannot be broken, even with unlimited computing power.

cards.title: XOR as a pad
cards.code:
msg = 0b1100
key = 0b1010
c = msg ^ key
print(bin(c))        # 0b110
print(bin(c ^ key))  # 0b1100
cards.body: XOR (^) flips the message bits wherever the key has a 1. Doing it again with the same key flips them back, because k ^ k = 0. Time O(n) and space O(n) for n bits.

cards.title: Tea with Turing
cards.body: In 1942 Alan Turing came to the US to inspect secret speech-scrambling work. He and Shannon met over tea in the Bell Labs cafeteria. They kept cryptography out of it entirely and talked instead about thinking machines and how the brain works.

cards.title: The 1948 paper
cards.body: In 1948 Shannon published "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" in two parts in the Bell System Technical Journal. To him, communication meant getting a copy of a chosen message to the far end. What the message means does not matter to that engineering job. A 1949 book version added an essay by Warren Weaver.

cards.title: Six boxes, one path
bullets: Source: makes the message.
Transmitter: turns it into a signal.
Channel: carries the signal.
Receiver: turns the signal back into a message.
Destination: who or what gets it.
cards.body: Shannon drew every link as the same boxes. A sixth box, the noise source, feeds into the channel and corrupts the signal.

cards.title: Information is choice
cards.body: Earlier Bell engineers, Nyquist (1924) and Hartley (1927), saw that information is about choice: what counts is how many messages you could have sent, not which one you did. A message picked from more possibilities carries more information.

cards.title: One bit
cards.body: A bit is the information in picking one of two outcomes that are equally likely, like a fair coin. John Tukey, a colleague, suggested the name at lunch. Each extra bit doubles the options, so n equally likely options take log2(n) bits.

cards.title: Measuring surprise
cards.body: Information is uncertainty that gets cleared up. If you already know the result, you learn nothing: a coin with heads on both sides gives 0 bits per flip. An outcome with probability p carries log2(1/p) bits of surprise, so rare outcomes surprise you more.

cards.title: The formula
cards.body: Entropy H is the average surprise: add up p · log2(1/p) over all outcomes. It is largest when all outcomes are equally likely; then n outcomes give log2(n) bits. A fair coin gives 1 bit, a fair 8-sided die 3 bits. The more lopsided the odds, the lower H.

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: Time O(k) for k outcomes, O(1) extra space.

cards.title: Lopsided coins
cards.body: A coin that lands heads 90% of the time gives about 0.47 bits per flip; at 99% it drops to about 0.08. Shannon's paper showed this curve: 1 bit at 50/50, falling to 0 at either extreme.

cards.title: Why "entropy"?
cards.body: The name borrows from physics, where entropy measures disorder. A famous story says John von Neumann told Shannon to use it; the book says that talk almost certainly never happened.

sources.title: A Mind at Play (Soni & Goodman, 2017), ch. 16

cards.title: The predictable part
cards.body: Redundancy is the part of a message you could have guessed from the rest, so it adds nothing new. In "Thank y_u" the missing letter is no mystery. Shannon estimated English is about half redundant, and later put it as high as 80%. Redundancy is also why codebreakers can crack ciphers: letter patterns leak through.

cards.title: Short codes, common symbols
cards.body: To compress, give frequent symbols short codewords and rare ones long codewords. Use a prefix code: no codeword is the start of another, so a stream of bits splits up only one way. The average length is the sum of p × (codeword length).

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: Time O(k) for k symbols. Entropy of this source is about 1.85 bits, so 1.9 is close but not perfect.

cards.title: The limit
cards.body: Shannon's first theorem: no code can average fewer bits per symbol than the source's entropy, and good codes get close to it. Shannon and Robert Fano built early codes; Fano's student David Huffman improved them. Building a Huffman code with a heap takes O(k log k) time for k symbols.

sources.title: A Mind at Play (Soni & Goodman, 2017), ch. 16

cards.title: The old answer
cards.body: Before Shannon, engineers fought noise mostly with power: send a stronger signal and shout over the static. Shannon turned this around. Leave the channel as it is and change how you encode the message, adding redundancy in a clever way.

cards.title: Channel capacity
cards.body: Every channel has a capacity: the most bits per second it can carry reliably. It depends on the channel's bandwidth and its signal-to-noise ratio. Shannon's second theorem: below capacity, good coding can make errors as rare as you like; above it, no code can. This speed limit is called the Shannon limit.

cards.title: A repetition code
cards.body: Send each bit 3 times and take a majority vote of each block. One flipped copy per block gets fixed. Time O(n), but it triples the bits.

cards.title: Finding the codes
cards.body: Shannon proved good codes must exist but didn't say how to build them. Smarter codes protect more for fewer extra bits, and the search took decades: in 1993 codes finally came close to the Shannon limit.

cards.title: Meeting Betty
cards.body: In fall 1948 Shannon met Betty Moore, an analyst at Bell Labs. They married on March 22, 1949. She did the wiring for the first version of his maze-solving mouse.

cards.title: Playful machines
bullets: Theseus: a mechanical mouse that learned its way through a maze; its memory was 75 telephone-style relays.
Ultimate Machine: flip its switch and a hand reaches out to switch it off.
THROBAC: a calculator that worked in Roman numerals.
A wearable computer, built with Ed Thorp, to predict roulette.

cards.title: Chess and MIT
cards.body: His paper "Programming a Computer for Playing Chess" set out ideas computer chess used for decades. In 1956 he went back to MIT as a visiting professor and became a full professor from 1957. The family named their house in Winchester Entropy House.

cards.title: Honors and prizes
bullets: 1959: put forward for the physics Nobel along with Norbert Wiener; the prize went to others, and there is no Nobel for mathematics.
1967: National Medal of Science, from President Johnson.
1985: the first Kyoto Prize in Basic Science.

cards.title: Last years
cards.body: In 1983 a doctor found he was probably in the very early stages of Alzheimer's disease. Betty cared for him at home for years. Claude Shannon died on February 24, 2001.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Big O describes how the work an algorithm does grows as its input grows. It counts steps, not seconds, so it compares algorithms rather than computers. n stands for the input size. The same notation is used for memory.

cards.title: Doubling the input
bullets: O(1): same time, whatever n is
O(log n): just one more step
O(n): about twice the time
O(n²): about four times the time

cards.title: Common run times
cards.body: From fastest to slowest:
bullets: O(1) constant: a dict lookup (on average)
O(log n) logarithmic: binary search
O(n) linear: scanning an unsorted list
O(n log n) linearithmic: merge sort
O(n²) quadratic: bubble sort. Slower still: O(2ⁿ), O(n!)

cards.title: Counting with logs
cards.body: Here log n means log base 2: how many times n can be halved before it reaches 1. log₂ 1,024 is 10, so a thousand items give about 10 halvings and a million about 20.

cards.title: Why growth matters
cards.body: Growth rates pull apart quickly. At a million items a log n method needs about 20 steps and a linear one a million. Code that feels instant on a test list can crawl on real data if its growth rate is bad.

cards.title: Single steps: O(1)
cards.body: A step whose cost doesn't depend on n is O(1): reading items[0], adding two numbers, returning a value. Indexing a list jumps straight to the slot, whether the list holds ten items or ten million.

cards.title: One loop: O(n)
cards.body: A loop that does O(1) work on each of n items takes n steps in total. It keeps only a variable or two, so its extra space is O(1).
cards.code:
for x in items:   # n passes
    print(x)      # O(1) each
# n × O(1) = O(n)

cards.title: Nested loops multiply
cards.body: A loop inside a loop runs its body once per outer pass. Two loops over n give n × n = n², three give n³. Over two lists of sizes n and m it is n × m, which is n² only when both have the same size.

cards.title: Triangle loops
cards.body: If the inner loop runs up to the outer index, it runs 0, 1, 2, … n − 1 times. That adds up to n(n − 1)/2, about half of n², which is still O(n²).

cards.title: Shapes to spot
bullets: Jump to one slot: O(1)
One pass over the input: O(n)
A loop in a loop: O(n²)
Halve (or double) until done: O(log n)
Try every subset (each item in or out): O(2ⁿ)

cards.title: Keep the big term
cards.body: Big O keeps only the term that grows fastest and drops the rest. For 4n³ + 2n + 9 the n³ term wins, so it is O(n³). At n = 1,000, n³ is a billion while 2n is only 2,000.

cards.title: Drop the multiplier
cards.body: Constant factors don't change the shape of growth. 7n steps, n/3 steps and n steps are all O(n): doubling n doubles each of them. Doing several steps per pass, or skipping every other item, still gives work that grows in a straight line.

cards.title: Add or multiply
cards.body: Loops one after another add their costs. Loops inside each other multiply them.
cards.code:
loop, then another loop
  n + n = 2n     -> O(n)
loop inside a loop
  n × n = n²     -> O(n²)
loop, then nested loops
  n + n²         -> O(n²)

cards.title: Rules of thumb
bullets: Drop constant factors: 5n becomes n
Drop smaller terms: n² + n becomes n²
Keep different inputs apart: n × m

cards.title: When constants matter
cards.body: Big O drops constants, but they are real work. If two algorithms have the same growth rate, the one with less work per step wins in practice. If their rates differ, the slower-growing one wins once n is big enough, however large its constant is.

cards.title: A worked example
cards.body: A takes 50·n steps, B takes n² steps. B wins on tiny inputs, they tie at n = 50, and after that A pulls away for good.

cards.title: Quicksort vs merge sort
cards.body: Both sort in O(n log n) on average. Quicksort usually finishes first because each step does less work: it partitions in place, so its hidden constant is smaller. Merge sort stays O(n log n) even in its worst case but needs O(n) extra memory.

cards.title: Best, worst, average
cards.body: The best case is the luckiest input, the worst case the unluckiest. A scan that stops at a match costs O(1) when the target is first and O(n) when it is last or missing. Big O usually quotes the worst case: a promise that it is never slower than that.

cards.title: Quicksort's cases
bullets: Every level of splitting touches all n items: O(n)
Even splits: about log n levels, O(n log n)
Pivot always smallest or largest: n levels, O(n²)
Random pivot: O(n log n) on average

cards.title: Halving loops
cards.body: A loop that cuts n in half on each pass runs about log₂ n times, because that is how many halvings take n down to 1. A counter that doubles from 1 up to n needs the same number of passes. Either way it keeps one counter: O(1) space.

cards.title: Log inside a loop
cards.body: Put a halving or doubling loop inside a loop that runs n times and you get n × log n, O(n log n). Multiplying works here because the inner loop does the same amount of work on every outer pass.

cards.title: When not to multiply
cards.body: If the inner work changes from pass to pass, add the passes up instead. When an inner loop runs 1, 2, 4, 8, … times up to n, the total 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n is less than 2n. That is O(n), even though the outer loop runs log n times.

cards.title: Memory grows too
cards.body: Space complexity measures the extra memory an algorithm needs on top of its input, with the same Big O rules. O(1) extra space means a fixed number of variables however large the input is. It doesn't mean zero memory or exactly one variable.

cards.title: O(1) vs O(n)
Running answers
cards.body: Many one-pass tasks only need a running answer: a sum, a count, the best value so far. They take O(n) time and O(1) space. Storing things you don't need wastes memory, and sorting first costs O(n log n) time.

cards.title: Merge sort's buffer
cards.body: Merge sort combines two sorted halves into a temporary list. That buffer can hold all n items, so merge sort needs O(n) extra space on top of its O(n log n) time.

cards.title: List operations
bullets: items[i], len(items): O(1)
append(x): O(1) amortized
x in items: O(n), it checks item by item
insert(0, x), pop(0): O(n), the rest shifts over
sorted(items): O(n log n)

cards.title: Sets and dicts
cards.body: Sets and dicts are hash tables. The hash of a key points straight to its slot, so lookup, insert and `in` are O(1) on average. In a rare worst case many keys collide and an operation degrades to O(n).

cards.title: Other handy tools
bullets: deque.appendleft(x), popleft(): O(1)
bisect.bisect(sorted_list, x): O(log n), a binary search
list.sort(): O(n log n)

cards.title: Amortized append
cards.body: A list keeps spare room at its end. When the room runs out, Python moves everything to a bigger block, which costs O(n). The new block is bigger by a share of the current size, so moves get rarer as the list grows: n appends cost O(n) in all, O(1) each on average.

cards.title: Fixed growth fails
cards.body: Growing by a fixed number of slots instead would mean a move every few appends, each copying everything so far. Those copies add up like 5 + 10 + 15 + … + n, which grows like n², so each append averages O(n). Growing in proportion to the size is what keeps append cheap.

sources.title: Python docs: Time complexity of built-in types

cards.title: Hidden loops
cards.body: `x in some_list` and `some_list.count(x)` are loops in disguise. Called inside another loop over n items they turn O(n) work into O(n²).

cards.title: Trade memory for time
cards.body: Build a set once and each membership test becomes O(1) on average. A set of values seen so far also answers 'have I met this before?' in one pass. O(n) time, O(n) space.

cards.title: Tallying with a dict
cards.body: A dict can count values in one pass: read the current count with a default of 0 and store one more. Each update is O(1) on average, so the pass is O(n) time, with O(k) space for k distinct values.

cards.title: Two pointers
cards.body: On a sorted list you can sometimes skip the extra memory. Start one index at each end. If the pair is too small move the low one up, if too big move the high one down. Each step rules out one item, so O(n) time and O(1) space.
cards.code:
a = [1, 3, 4, 6, 9], want 13
1 + 9 = 10  too small: lo up
3 + 9 = 12  too small: lo up
4 + 9 = 13  found
