cards.title: Time: count the calls
cards.body: For recursion, time is about (number of calls) × (work per call). A function that calls itself once on n − 1 makes about n calls. One that calls itself once on n // 2 makes about log₂ n calls.

cards.title: Space: stack depth
cards.body: Every call waits on the call stack until the call it made returns. Extra space is the longest chain of waiting calls, not the total number of calls. Shrinking by one gives depth n, O(n). Halving gives depth log n, O(log n).

cards.title: Hidden copies
cards.body: A slice like items[1:] builds a new list on every call. Over n calls the copies hold n − 1, n − 2, … items, about n²/2 steps, so the time is O(n²). Passing a start index instead keeps it O(n).

cards.title: Two calls on halves
cards.body: If each call does O(1) work but calls itself twice on half the input, the call tree has 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n nodes, about 2n, so it is O(n) time with a stack only log n deep. Compute the half once and reuse it, and there is one call per level: O(log n).

cards.title: Writing T(n)
cards.body: A recurrence gives a recursive algorithm's cost in terms of smaller inputs. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) reads: two calls on halves, plus linear work to combine them. T(n/2) + O(1) is one call on a half plus constant work: log n levels, O(log n).

cards.title: Levels times work
cards.body: Picture the call tree, count its levels and the work on each level, then add it up. Merge sort halves the list, so there are about log₂ n levels, and the merges on each level touch all n items. n work on log n levels is O(n log n) in every case.

cards.title: Shrinking by one
cards.body: When each call shrinks n by 1 there are n levels. With O(1) work per level that is O(n). If each level scans what is left, the work is n + (n − 1) + … + 1, about n²/2: O(n²).

cards.title: Branching blows up
cards.body: A call that makes two calls which each shrink by only one doubles the number of calls per level: 1, 2, 4, 8, … about 2ⁿ in total. Naive recursive Fibonacci works like this, which is why it takes exponential time.

cards.title: Caching fixes it
cards.body: When branches recompute the same inputs, store each result the first time. functools.cache does it for you. Each input is then computed once: at most (r + 1)(c + 1) of them instead of an exponential number of calls.

cards.title: Every ordering
cards.body: Some problems seem to need every ordering. With n stops there are n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 1 orders: 4 stops give 24, 9 give 362,880. Each extra stop multiplies the count by the new n. Measuring every route is O(n · n!), worse even than O(2ⁿ).
cards.code:
from itertools import permutations
stops = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
orders = list(permutations(stops))
print(len(orders))   # 24

cards.title: NP-complete problems
cards.body: The traveling salesperson problem (the shortest tour through every stop) and set cover (the fewest groups that cover everything) are NP-complete. Nobody knows a fast exact algorithm for them, and most experts think none exists. Brute force set cover tries all 2ⁿ subsets.

cards.title: Warning signs
bullets: Fast with a few items, hopeless with a few dozen
You must try every combination, order or subset
A route through many points (one A-to-B path is easy)
A known hard problem, like set cover, hides inside it

cards.title: Approximation algorithms
cards.body: When the exact answer would take too long, use an approximation algorithm: fast and close to the best, but with no promise that it is the best. They are judged by speed and by how close they get. Greedy rules make good ones, like always driving to the nearest unvisited stop.

cards.title: Words to know
bullets: Brute force: try every possible answer
Factorial time: grows like n!
Greedy: take the best-looking choice right now

cards.title: Why sort
cards.body: Sorting puts items in order so later jobs get easier: binary search, spotting duplicates, ranking. Most simple sorts work in passes. A pass is one sweep through the list.

cards.title: Stable sorts
cards.body: A sort is stable when items that count as equal keep the order they had before. Sort a hand of cards by rank: with a stable sort, two 7s stay in their old left-to-right order. This matters when you sort by one field and then by another.

cards.title: More words
bullets: In place: rearranges the list itself, using only O(1) extra memory.
Adaptive: runs faster when the input is already nearly sorted.
Pivot: the item quicksort splits the list around.
Pass: one sweep through the list.

cards.title: Is it sorted?
cards.body: Compare each item with the one after it. One pair out of order means the list is not sorted, so you can stop right there. With an index loop, stop at len(a) - 1 so a[i + 1] stays inside the list. Time O(n), extra space O(1).
cards.code:
def is_sorted(a):
    return all(x <= y for x, y
               in zip(a, a[1:]))

print(is_sorted([1, 4, 4, 9]))

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Find the smallest item in the unsorted part and swap it to the front of that part. Then do the same for the rest. After pass i, the first i + 1 items are in their final places.

cards.title: Passes traced
cards.body: Pass 1 swaps 7 with 41; nothing else moves. In pass 2, 18 is already the smallest, so it stays.

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: m holds the index of the smallest item seen so far in this pass.

cards.title: A new-list version
cards.body: You can also copy the list, then keep finding its smallest item with min(), taking it out with remove() (which deletes the first copy) and appending it to a new list. Each round is O(n), so it is still O(n²) time, but it needs O(n) extra space.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Big O drops the 1/2: O(n²) time in the best, average and worst case, even on sorted input.
At most n - 1 swaps; O(1) extra space.
Not stable: a long swap can jump an item over its twin, e.g. [5a, 5b, 2] becomes [2, 5b, 5a].

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Walk along the list comparing neighbors and swap any pair where the left one is bigger. The largest item wins every comparison, so one pass carries it to the end. After pass i, the last i + 1 items are final, so each pass can stop earlier.

cards.title: One pass traced
cards.body: 9 reached the end. The small 1 moved only one step left.

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: a, b = b, a swaps two values in one line. j stops at n - 2 - i, so a[j + 1] stays inside the list and the sorted tail is skipped. A pass with no swaps means the list is sorted, so we stop early.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Without the early exit: (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons, about n²/2.
Best case O(n) with the early exit: a sorted list takes one pass of n - 1 comparisons.
Average and worst case O(n²); extra space O(1).
Stable, because it swaps only when the left item is strictly bigger (> not >=).

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Keep a sorted part on the left. Take the next item (the key), shift every bigger item in the sorted part one slot right, and drop the key into the gap. It is how many people sort cards in their hand.

cards.title: One insert traced
cards.body: The 6 has not been touched yet; it is the next key.

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: The while loop stops at index -1 or at an item that is not bigger than key. The gap is then at j + 1.

cards.title: Counting shifts
cards.body: Every shift fixes one pair of items that were out of order. A reversed list has the most such pairs, n(n - 1)/2: for [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] that is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 shifts. A sorted list needs 0 shifts.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Best case O(n) on sorted input; average and worst case O(n²).
O(1) extra space, stable, and adaptive.
The best simple choice for short or nearly sorted lists.

cards.title: Divide and conquer
cards.body: Divide and conquer (D&C) is a recursive way to solve problems. First find a base case so simple you can answer it straight away. Then find a way to split or shrink the problem until it reaches that base case. Binary search, merge sort and quicksort all work this way.

cards.title: The plan
cards.body: Split the list in half, sort each half with merge sort, then merge the two sorted halves. A list of 0 or 1 items is already sorted: that is the base case. Halving 16 items goes 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: four levels, because 2⁴ = 16. In general there are log₂ n levels.

cards.title: Merging two halves
cards.body: Look only at the front item of each sorted half and take the smaller one. Repeat until one half is empty, then add the rest of the other. On a tie take the left item (<=), so equal items keep their order and the sort stays stable.

cards.title: The recursion
cards.body: Use // so mid is a whole number. Checking only len(a) == 0 would recurse forever on a 1-item list.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Each level merges n items in total: O(n) per level.
log n levels × O(n) = O(n log n) in the best, average and worst case.
O(n) extra space for the merged lists, so it is not in place.
Stable.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Pick one item as the pivot. Partition: move smaller items to its left and the rest to its right. The pivot is now in its final place. Sort the two sides the same way. Lists with fewer than 2 items are the base case. The sides are partitioned, not yet sorted.

cards.title: Easy version
cards.code:
def quicksort(a):
    if len(a) < 2:
        return a
    p = a[0]
    rest = a[1:]
    s = [x for x in rest if x < p]
    b = [x for x in rest if x >= p]
    return (quicksort(s) + [p]
            + quicksort(b))
cards.body: Using >= keeps copies of the pivot; with > they would vanish. A middle group [x for x in a if x == p] also keeps them. Any item can be the pivot: the middle value a[len(a) // 2] avoids bad splits on sorted input. New lists mean O(n) extra space.

cards.title: In-place partition
cards.body: The last item is the pivot. i marks where the next small item goes. The final swap drops the pivot between the groups. O(n) time, O(1) space.

cards.title: The recursion
cards.body: Both calls leave out index p, because the pivot is already in place. Passing p again could repeat the same range forever.

cards.title: Work per level
cards.body: Picture the recursion as levels. On every level, the partitions together touch about all n items, so each level costs O(n). Total time is n times the number of levels.

cards.title: Good and bad splits
bullets: Even splits: about log n levels, so O(n log n) time and O(log n) stack.
Pivot is always the smallest or largest: sides of 0 and n - 1, so n levels: O(n²) time, O(n) stack.
A first-item pivot on a list that is already sorted does exactly that.

cards.title: Choosing a pivot
cards.body: Use the middle item or a random one. With a random pivot no fixed input can force bad splits every time, so the expected time is O(n log n). The worst case can still happen, but it is very unlikely. random.randint(lo, hi) includes both ends; swap the chosen item to the end, then partition.

cards.title: Many duplicates
cards.body: A three-way partition makes three groups: less than, equal to, and greater than the pivot. The equal group is done and never sorted again, so a list of all-equal items takes O(n). It does not fix a bad pivot on sorted input.

cards.title: Versus merge sort
cards.body: Both are O(n log n) on average. Quicksort is usually faster in practice: its constant factor is smaller (little copying, works in place), and with random pivots it almost always hits the average case. Merge sort wins when you need a guarantee or stability. Quicksort is not stable.

cards.title: What a heap is
cards.body: A max-heap is a tree where every parent is at least as big as its children, so the largest item is at the root. It fits in a plain list with no pointers: the root is at index 0, the children of i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent is at (i - 1) // 2.

cards.title: Sift down
cards.body: Swap a[i] with its bigger child until it is bigger than both. O(log n), since a heap has about log n levels.

cards.title: Heapsort steps
cards.body: Build the heap from the last parent back to the root: O(n). Then swap the max to the end, shrink the heap by one, and repair the root.

cards.title: With heapq
cards.body: Python's heapq is a min-heap. heapify(a) builds it in O(n); heappop(a) removes the smallest item in O(log n). Popping n times gives sorted order, but into a new list: O(n) extra space.
cards.code:
import heapq
h = [5, 1, 4]
heapq.heapify(h)
print([heapq.heappop(h)
       for _ in range(len(h))])

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: O(n log n) time in the best, average and worst case.
O(1) extra space for the in-place version.
Not stable.
The usual pick when you need a guarantee and no extra memory.

cards.title: Count, don't compare
cards.body: For whole numbers from 0 to k, counting sort tallies how often each value appears in a list of k + 1 counters, then writes each value out that many times. Example: [3, 1, 3, 0] with k = 3 gives counts [1, 1, 0, 2], which reads back as [0, 1, 3, 3].

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: k + 1 slots, so the value k has a slot of its own.

cards.title: Cost and fit
bullets: O(n + k) time and O(n + k) space in every case; k is the size of the value range.
No item is ever compared with another.
Great when k is small next to n, like many scores from 0 to 100.
Poor when k is huge next to n: 5 numbers up to a billion means a billion counters.

cards.title: Radix sort
cards.body: Sort by the ones digit, then the tens, then higher digits. 23 and 13 tie on the ones digit and keep their order (23 first).

cards.title: Why passes must be stable
cards.body: When two numbers share the current digit, their order must still show the lower digits sorted earlier. An unstable pass could scramble them. So each pass uses a stable sort, usually counting sort. With d digits and k digit values: O(d × (n + k)) time, O(n + k) space.

cards.title: sorted vs sort
cards.body: sorted(x) returns a new list and works on any iterable, even a string (sorted("tea") gives ['a', 'e', 't']). list.sort() sorts the list itself and returns None, so writing result = nums.sort() leaves result as None.

cards.title: key and reverse
cards.code:
names = ["Zoe", "al", "Bea"]
print(sorted(names, key=str.lower))
print(sorted([4, 9, 1],
             reverse=True))
print(sorted(["aaa", "b"], key=len))
cards.body: key takes a function that gives the value to sort by. reverse=True flips the order. Output: ['al', 'Bea', 'Zoe'], [9, 4, 1], ['b', 'aaa'].

cards.title: How Timsort works
cards.body: Python sorts with Timsort, a blend of merge sort and insertion sort. It first finds runs that are already in order, sorts short pieces with insertion sort, and merges the runs. A sorted list is one long run: n - 1 comparisons and nothing to merge.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Best case O(n) on sorted input.
Average and worst case O(n log n).
Up to O(n) extra space.
Stable.

cards.title: Stability in use
cards.code:
pets = [("rex", 3), ("ida", 1),
        ("bo", 3), ("kit", 1)]
by_age = sorted(pets,
                key=lambda p: p[1])
print([p[0] for p in by_age])
cards.body: Prints ['ida', 'kit', 'rex', 'bo']: age 1 first, and pets with the same age stay in their original order.

cards.title: Core ideas
bullets: Bubble: compare neighbors and swap any out-of-order pair.
Selection: each pass, find the minimum of the rest and put it next.
Insertion: grow a sorted left part one item at a time.
Merge: halve, sort both halves, merge them. Quick: split around a pivot item.
Heap: keep removing the max from a heap. Counting: count each value.

cards.title: Costs side by side
bullets: Bubble, selection, insertion: O(n²) average and worst, O(1) space. Insertion is O(n) best.
Merge: O(n log n) always, O(n) extra space, stable.
Heap: O(n log n) always, O(1) extra space, not stable.
Quick: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, O(log n) stack.
Counting: O(n + k), no comparisons.

cards.title: The n log n floor
cards.body: A sort that only learns by comparing two items must, in the worst case, make about n log n comparisons. There are n! possible orders, and each yes/no comparison can at best halve the orders still possible. log₂(n!) grows like n log₂ n. Counting and radix sort dodge this by not comparing.

cards.title: Which to pick
bullets: Small, almost-sorted input: insertion sort, close to O(n).
Need stable and a guaranteed O(n log n): merge sort.
Need that guarantee with O(1) extra memory: heapsort.
Many whole numbers in a tiny range: counting sort.
Speed on average, in place, stability not needed: quicksort.

sources.title: GeeksforGeeks: Lower bound for comparison sorts

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Check the items one by one from the start and stop at the first match. It works on any list, sorted or not. It is also called simple search. A missing item is only known to be missing after every item has been checked.

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: Return -1 only after the loop, once nothing matched. == compares; a single = assigns. A yes/no version returns True inside the loop and False after it.

cards.title: Python does it too
bullets: x in some_list checks items one by one from index 0.
[4, 7, 4].index(4) gives 0, the first match.
"dog".find("x") gives -1 when the text is missing.
min() and max() scan every item.

cards.title: Finding the smallest
cards.body: Start with best = a[0], then look at every item and replace best whenever you see a smaller one. Flip the test to > and you get the largest instead. This search can never stop early, so it is O(n) in every case.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Best case O(1): the target is the first item.
Worst case O(n): the target is last or missing, e.g. 10 checks for 10 items.
O(1) extra space.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: On a sorted list, look at the middle item. If it is the target, you are done. If it is bigger than the target, everything to its right is bigger too, so only the left half can hold the target. If it is smaller, keep the right half. Each check throws away half. Unsorted data breaks this.

cards.title: Counting halvings
cards.body: n items shrink to 1 after about log₂ n halvings, because 2 multiplied by itself log₂ n times is n. In the worst case binary search checks ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 items. About a million items: 20 checks. About a billion: 30.
cards.code:
import math
print(math.log2(1024))  # 10.0
print(2 ** 20)  # 1048576

cards.title: Simple vs binary
cards.body: Doubling the list adds n more checks to simple search but only 1 more to binary search. Going from 500 to 1,000 items, the worst case for simple search grows from 500 to 1,000 checks; binary search goes from 9 to 10. The bigger the list, the wider the gap.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Best case O(1): the first middle is the target.
Average and worst case O(log n).
O(1) extra space for the loop version.
Sorting first costs O(n log n), so for a single search of unsorted data a linear scan is cheaper.

cards.title: The loop
cards.body: lo and hi mark the part of the list that can still hold the target.

cards.title: Why each piece
bullets: // rounds down to a whole number. / gives a float, which can't be an index.
lo <= hi: when lo == hi one item is still left to check.
mid + 1 and mid - 1: a[mid] is already ruled out, so leave it out.
lo > hi means the range is empty: the target is missing.

cards.title: A miss traced
cards.code:
find 10 in [2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 14]
lo=0 hi=5 mid=2:  6 < 10, lo=3
lo=3 hi=5 mid=4: 12 > 10, hi=3
lo=3 hi=3 mid=3:  8 < 10, lo=4
lo > hi: return -1
cards.body: Checks 6, 12, 8, then stops.

cards.title: Recursive version
cards.body: Same O(log n) time, but each call waits on the stack: O(log n) space instead of O(1).

cards.title: Two classic bugs
bullets: lo = mid instead of mid + 1: with lo = 0, hi = 1, mid stays 0 and the loop never ends.
while lo < hi with hi = len(a) - 1: the last item left is never checked, so search([1, 2], 2) returns -1.

cards.title: Insert positions
cards.body: Often you want where a value belongs, not just whether it is there. bisect_left(a, x) gives the first index whose item is >= x: before any copies of x. bisect_right(a, x) gives the first index whose item is > x: after the copies. Both are binary searches.
cards.code:
import bisect
a = [2, 4, 4, 4, 7]
print(bisect.bisect_left(a, 4))
print(bisect.bisect_right(a, 4))
print(bisect.bisect_left(a, 5))

cards.title: Reading the output
cards.body: The code prints 1, 4 and 4. The three 4s sit at indexes 1 to 3, so the left edge is 1 and the right edge is one past them, 4. 5 is missing; it would go before 7, at index 4.

cards.title: Writing lower bound
cards.body: hi starts at len(a), one past the end, for "no item is big enough". hi = mid keeps mid as a candidate, so the loop is lo < hi. When it ends, lo is the answer.

cards.title: What it's good for
bullets: First copy of x: bisect_left. Last copy: bisect_right minus 1.
How many copies of x: bisect_right minus bisect_left.
Smallest stored value >= x: a[bisect_left(a, x)]. A hash set can't answer this, since it keeps no order.
Each call is O(log n) time and O(1) space.

cards.title: Jump to the bucket
cards.body: A set or dict hashes the value to find its bucket directly, so x in some_set is O(1) on average, while x in some_list scans: O(n). Building a set from n items costs O(n) time and O(n) space once; after that every check is cheap.

cards.title: The worst case
cards.body: If many keys land in the same bucket (collisions), a lookup has to look through all of them: O(n) in the worst case. Good hash functions spread keys out, so this is rare.

cards.title: Seen it before?
cards.body: Check before you add, or every item looks like a repeat. Sets use .add, lists use .append. O(n) time and O(n) space; comparing every pair would be O(n²) time but O(1) space.

cards.title: Pair sum, unsorted
cards.body: To find two numbers adding to a target, walk the list once. For each x, the partner you need is target - x. Keep a dict from each number seen so far to its index. Target 10 in [3, 8, 7]: at 7 you need 3, which was seen at index 0. One pass: O(n) time, O(n) space.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: To find a pair with a given sum in a sorted list, put one pointer at each end. Sum too small: move the left pointer right to a bigger item. Sum too big: move the right pointer left to a smaller item. Stop when they meet, so an item is never paired with itself.

cards.title: In Python
What it costs
bullets: Each step moves one pointer inward, so at most n - 1 steps: O(n) time.
O(1) extra space.
Checking every pair instead: O(n²).
Needs sorted data; sorting first adds O(n log n).

cards.title: Fixed-size window
cards.body: For sums of k neighbors in a row, don't add up every window from scratch, which costs O(n · k). Slide instead: add the item that enters and subtract the one that leaves. When a[i] enters, a[i - k] falls out. Each slide is O(1), so the whole scan is O(n) with O(1) space.

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
def best_window(a, k):
    w = sum(a[:k])
    best = w
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        w += a[i] - a[i - k]
        best = max(best, w)
    return best

a = [2, 7, 1, 8, 3]
print(best_window(a, 3))
cards.body: Windows of 3: 10, 16, 12. Prints 16.

cards.title: Grow and shrink
bullets: For a window of any size over positive numbers: hi moves right, adding a[hi].
While the window breaks the rule (say, sum > k): subtract a[lo] first, then lo += 1.
Now lo..hi is valid and holds hi - lo + 1 items.
Each index enters once and leaves at most once: O(n) time despite the inner loop, O(1) space.

cards.title: What rotation does
cards.body: A rotated list is a sorted list cut in two with the pieces swapped, like [10, 12, 15, 1, 3, 6]. It has exactly one drop (15 to 1). Pick any middle: the drop sits on at most one side, so at least one half is in sorted order.

cards.title: The rule
bullets: If a[lo] <= a[mid], the left half is sorted. The = matters: when lo == mid, the left half is one item, which is sorted.
Otherwise the right half is sorted.
Is the target inside the sorted half's range? Search there; if not, search the other half.
Half is dropped each step: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

cards.title: Which half
cards.body: The right half [1, 2, 3] is sorted, 6 is not in it, so go left.

cards.title: Smallest item
cards.body: The smallest item sits just after the drop. Compare a[mid] with a[hi]. If a[mid] > a[hi], the drop is right of mid: lo = mid + 1. Else the minimum is at mid or left of it: hi = mid. Loop while lo < hi. Comparing with a[lo] instead fails on a list that isn't rotated. [9, 11, 2, 4, 6] gives 2.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Sometimes you search a range of possible answers, not a list: a speed, a size, a capacity. Suppose a yes/no check ok(x) is False for every x that is too small and True from some point on. Then binary search can find that switch point: if ok(mid), the answer is mid or lower; if not, it is higher.

cards.title: An example
cards.body: Slowest pages-per-day rate that reads each chapter in ps within the days (one chapter per day at most). -(-p//r) divides, rounding up. Prints 12.

cards.title: Round the middle up
cards.body: When you want the largest x that passes, the update is lo = mid. Then mid must round up, (lo + hi + 1) // 2. Otherwise, once hi = lo + 1, mid equals lo, nothing changes and the loop never ends.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: About log₂(range) checks. For answers 1 to M: about log₂ M.
If one check scans n items: O(n log M) time.
M = 1,000,000,000 needs only about 30 checks.
Trying every value instead: O(n · M). Extra space O(1).

cards.title: Search in rings
cards.body: Breadth-first search (BFS) searches a graph outward from a start node: first every node 1 step away, then every node 2 steps away, and so on. It answers two questions: is there a path to the goal, and which path has the fewest steps? Depth-first search instead follows one path as far as it goes before backing up.

cards.title: Why a queue
cards.body: BFS keeps the nodes still to check in a queue: first in, first out. Nodes come back out in the order they were found, so all near nodes are checked before far ones, and the first time the goal comes out its distance is the smallest. A stack (last in, first out) would dive deep first and could find a longer path first.

cards.title: Mark what you've seen
cards.body: In a graph with a cycle (A to B and B back to A), a node can be added to the queue again and again. That wastes work and can loop forever. Keep a set of seen nodes and add each node to the queue only once.

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: Each queue entry carries its distance; a neighbor is one step farther.

cards.title: Cost and limits
bullets: Time O(V + E): every node and edge is handled once. Space O(V).
Fewest steps means fewest edges, not lowest total cost.
When edges have different costs, such as road lengths, use Dijkstra's algorithm instead.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: k-nearest neighbors (kNN) answers a question about a new item by finding the k stored items most like it. Classification: let them vote and take the most common label, like spam or not spam. Regression: average their numbers to predict a number, like a price.

cards.title: Items as features
cards.body: To compare items, turn each one into a list of numbers called features. A used car might be (age in years, thousands of km driven). Pick features that relate to what you want to predict. Put them on similar scales (for example 0 to 1), or the feature with the biggest numbers swamps the rest.

cards.title: Measuring distance
cards.body: Straight-line distance: square each difference, add them, take the square root. Prints 5.0. It works for any number of features. math.dist does the same.

cards.title: Picking k
bullets: k = 1 trusts a single neighbor, which may be noise.
A bigger k gives smoother, steadier answers.
k = all items always predicts the overall most common label.
With two labels, an odd k means the vote can't tie.

cards.title: Voting in Python
cards.code:
from collections import Counter
near = ["spam", "ok", "spam"]
votes = Counter(near)
print(votes.most_common(1))
print(votes.most_common(1)[0][0])
cards.body: Sort the stored items by their distance to the new one and keep the first k. Counter tallies their labels; most_common(1) gives a list with the top (label, count) pair. Prints [('spam', 2)], then spam.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: No real training: just store the n items, O(n · d) space for d features.
Each prediction computes n distances: O(n · d).
Sorting them to find the k nearest: O(n log n).
Slow for huge data sets, since every query looks at everything.

cards.title: The toolbox
bullets: Linear search: look at each item in turn; no order needed. O(n).
Binary search: cut a sorted range in half every step. O(log n).
Two pointers: one index at each end, moving inward. O(n).
Sliding window: keep a running total as a range of neighbors moves along. O(n).
Hash lookup: hash the key to go directly to its bucket. O(1) average.

cards.title: Sort first?
cards.body: Sorting costs O(n log n), more than one O(n) scan. For a single search of unsorted data, just scan. For many searches, sort once and then each binary search is O(log n). Trying every pair of items is O(n²), which these tools usually avoid.

cards.title: Spot the pattern
bullets: Minimum size that still succeeds, when anything larger succeeds too: binary search over the answer range.
Sorted data that was cut and swapped: binary search that tests which half is in order.
Longest stretch of neighbors under a limit: a window that grows and shrinks.
Fewest moves through a maze or network: BFS, O(V + E).
Membership checks, like a name seen already: a hash set.

cards.title: Nodes and edges
cards.body: A graph is a set of things, called nodes or vertices, joined by links called edges. Two nodes joined by an edge are neighbors. The degree of a node is how many edges touch it. Road maps, friend networks and task lists are all graphs.

cards.title: Kinds of graphs
bullets: Directed: every edge is a one-way arrow (a follows b).
Undirected: every edge works both ways (a and b are cousins).
Weighted: every edge carries a cost, like minutes or dollars.
Connected: every node can reach every other node.
Sparse: far fewer edges than possible pairs of nodes.

cards.title: Paths and cycles
cards.body: A path is a chain of edges leading from one node to another. A cycle is a path that ends at the node where it started. Searches have to watch out for cycles, or they can walk around one forever.

cards.title: Trees are graphs
cards.body: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles, so there is exactly one path between any two nodes. With n nodes it always has n − 1 edges: every node except the root hangs from one edge to its parent. An extra edge between two nodes that are already linked would create a second path, which is a cycle.

cards.title: Degree in Python
cards.body: When each node maps to a list of its neighbors, len() of that list is the node's degree, in O(1) time.

cards.title: Adjacency list
cards.body: Keep a dict that maps each node to a list of its neighbors. Memory is O(V + E): one entry per node plus one per edge. Listing a node's neighbors is quick, but checking for one particular edge means scanning that node's list, O(degree).

cards.title: Adding edges
cards.code:
g = {n: [] for n in 'xyz'}
g['x'].append('y')  # x -> y
g['y'].append('z')  # y -> z
g['z'].append('y')  # z -> y
print(g)
cards.body: A directed edge u → v is stored once, in u's list. An undirected edge is stored in both lists, so the list lengths add up to twice the number of edges.

cards.title: Adjacency matrix
cards.body: A V × V grid where m[u][v] is 1 when the edge u → v exists (or holds its weight). Checking one edge reads a single cell, O(1). Listing a node's neighbors scans its whole row, O(V). Memory is O(V²) even when almost no edges exist. For an undirected graph the grid is mirrored across its diagonal.

cards.title: Which one to pick
bullets: Sparse graph (few edges per node): adjacency list.
Dense graph, or many "is u linked to v?" checks: matrix.
Edges in an undirected list: add up all list lengths, then halve. O(V).
Most graph algorithms assume an adjacency list.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: BFS spreads out from the start in rings: first every node one edge away, then every node two edges away, and so on. So the first time it reaches a node, it used the fewest possible edges. That makes BFS the tool for "is there a path?" and for shortest paths in an unweighted graph.

cards.title: Why a queue
cards.body: Nodes must be handled in the order they were found, so BFS keeps them in a first-in, first-out queue: take from the front, add to the back. In Python use collections.deque, whose popleft() is O(1); list.pop(0) is O(n). Taking from the back instead (a stack) turns it into depth-first search.

cards.title: Remember what you saw
cards.body: Keep a set of the nodes already found and mark each node as you add it to the queue. Without it, a node reachable two ways is handled twice, and a cycle keeps the search going around forever.

cards.title: In Python
What it costs
cards.body: Every node enters and leaves the queue once, O(V) in total, and every edge is checked once when its node leaves, O(E). So BFS on an adjacency list is O(V + E) time; when edges far outnumber nodes, the edge checks are most of the work. Space is O(V). On a matrix each neighbor lookup scans a full row, so BFS becomes O(V²).

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: DFS follows one path as deep as it can, then backs up to the latest fork and tries the next branch. It runs on a stack (last in, first out): either a list with append() and pop(), or the call stack through recursion. It reaches every node it can, but not by the shortest route.

cards.title: With a stack
cards.code:
g = {1: [2, 3], 2: [4],
     3: [], 4: []}
stack, seen = [1], set()
while stack:
    node = stack.pop()
    if node in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(node)
    print(node, end=' ')
    stack.extend(g[node])
# 1 3 2 4
cards.body: pop() takes the newest node, so the last neighbor pushed is explored first.

cards.title: With recursion
cards.body: Mark the node before visiting its neighbors, so a cycle can't loop forever. The recursion can get V calls deep.

cards.title: Counting components
cards.body: A connected component is a group of nodes that can all reach each other; a node with no edges is a component by itself. Loop over every node and start a new DFS (or BFS) from each one that no earlier search reached. Each new start is one more component.

cards.title: Spotting cycles
bullets: Undirected: every edge shows up from both ends, so seeing the node you came from proves nothing.
Undirected: any other already-seen neighbor means a cycle.
Directed: track unvisited, in progress (on the current path) and finished.
Directed: an edge to an in-progress node closes a cycle; one to a finished node does not.

cards.title: What it costs
cards.body: O(V + E) time with an adjacency list, like BFS: each node is handled once and each edge looked at once. O(V) space for the seen set plus the stack or recursion.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Let an arrow a → b mean "a must happen before b". A topological sort lists every node so that each one comes before all the nodes it points to, like courses before the courses that need them. Several orders are often valid. It only works on a directed graph with no cycles (a DAG): in a cycle each task waits on another forever.

cards.title: Kahn: count indegrees
cards.body: The indegree of a node is how many arrows point into it: how many prerequisites it still waits on.

cards.title: Kahn: the main loop
cards.body: Continues the card before. Nodes with nothing left to wait on start in the queue; taking one out lowers the count of each node it points to.

cards.title: The DFS way
cards.body: Run DFS and append a node to a list only after the loop over its neighbors ends, so everything it points to is already in the list. Reverse the list at the end: now every node comes before the nodes it points to.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Kahn's and the DFS way: O(V + E) time, O(V) space.
If Kahn's order holds fewer nodes than the graph, the rest sit on a cycle.
Uses: build steps, course plans, spreadsheet cells.

cards.title: Cheapest, not fewest
cards.body: BFS finds the route with the fewest edges, but with costs on the edges the cheapest route can use more of them. Dijkstra's algorithm finds the cheapest total cost from a start to every node. Repeat: pick the unfinished node with the smallest known cost, call it finished, and try to improve its neighbors through it.

cards.title: Dijkstra setup
cards.code:
from heapq import heappop, heappush
g = {'s': [('a', 7), ('b', 2)],
     'b': [('a', 3)], 'a': []}
INF = float('inf')
dist = {n: INF for n in g}
dist['s'] = 0
h = [(0, 's')]  # (distance, node)
cards.body: Distances start at infinity. The heap holds (distance, node) pairs, so it orders them by distance.

cards.title: The main loop
cards.body: Continues the setup. Relaxing: when going through node is cheaper, save the new cost and push it. Old pairs for that node stay in the heap and are skipped when popped.

cards.title: Rebuilding the route
cards.body: Each time you improve a node n, also save parent[n] = node. The start's parent is None. To get the route, begin at the goal and keep stepping to the parent, collecting nodes until you run out. The list is goal-first, so reverse it.

cards.title: Negative edges break it
cards.body: A finished node is never revisited. That is safe only if no later detour can be cheaper, which holds when all weights are 0 or more: any other route already costs at least as much before it even arrives. A negative edge can make a costlier detour end up cheaper, and the finished node misses it. Use Bellman-Ford then.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: With a min-heap: O((V + E) log V) time, O(V + E) space.
Scanning every node for the cheapest instead: O(V²) time.
Works on directed or undirected graphs, cycles included, when no weight is negative.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Bellman-Ford finds cheapest paths from a start even when some edges are negative. It has no heap and never calls a node finished. It simply relaxes every edge, round after round, keeping any shorter distance it finds.

cards.title: Why V − 1 rounds
cards.body: A cheapest path never needs to visit a node twice, so it has at most V − 1 edges. Each full round over all edges locks in at least one more edge of every cheapest path. After V − 1 rounds every distance is correct.

cards.title: In Python
Negative cycles
cards.body: Run one extra round. If any distance still drops, some loop has a negative total: going around it again keeps lowering the cost, so no cheapest path exists. That extra round is how Bellman-Ford reports a reachable negative cycle.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Time O(V × E): V − 1 rounds over E edges.
Space O(V) for the distances.
Slower than Dijkstra's, so use it when negative edges exist.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Union-find (disjoint sets) tracks which items belong together while groups keep merging. Each item points to a parent, and following parents up leads to the group's root, which names the group. Two items share a group exactly when they have the same root.

cards.title: In Python
Path compression
cards.body: While find walks up to the root, it points each node it passes straight at the root. That is the line parent[x] = find(parent[x]). Later finds from those nodes take a single step.

cards.title: Union by rank
cards.body: Keep a rank (a bound on height) for each root. When joining two groups, hang the root with the lower rank under the one with the higher rank, so the tree doesn't get taller. Only when the ranks are equal does the new root's rank go up by 1. That alone keeps every tree O(log n) tall.

cards.title: What it costs
cards.body: With both tricks, each find or union takes nearly constant amortized time; the bound grows so slowly it stays below 5 for any real input. Without them a group can become a long chain and one find can cost O(n). Space is O(n) for parent and rank.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: A spanning tree of a connected, undirected, weighted graph links all V nodes with V − 1 edges and no cycles. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is one whose edge weights add up to the least possible. Think of laying cable to reach every building as cheaply as possible.

cards.title: Kruskal's algorithm
bullets: Sort the edges from cheapest to dearest.
Keep an edge unless its two ends are already in one group (it would close a cycle).
Union-find makes that check fast.
Stop once V − 1 edges are kept.

cards.title: Kruskal in Python
cards.code:
# union() from the union-find note
E = [('a', 'b', 4), ('b', 'c', 1),
     ('a', 'c', 2), ('c', 'd', 5)]
E.sort(key=lambda e: e[2])
tree = []
for u, v, w in E:
    if union(u, v):
        tree.append((u, v, w))
print(tree)  # b-c, a-c, c-d: 8

cards.title: Prim's algorithm
cards.body: Prim's grows a single tree from a start node. At each step it adds the cheapest edge that joins a node in the tree to a node outside it. A min-heap of candidate edges makes that pick fast. Kruskal's and Prim's always reach the same minimum total weight.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Kruskal's: O(E log E) time, mostly the sort; O(V) for union-find.
Prim's with a heap: O(E log V) time, O(V + E) space.
Every spanning tree on V nodes has exactly V − 1 edges.

cards.title: Path problems
bullets: Fewest hops, no weights: BFS with a queue.
Cheapest route, weights 0 or more: Dijkstra's with a min-heap.
Cheapest route with negative weights: Bellman-Ford.
Reach everything, count components, find cycles: DFS with a stack or recursion.

cards.title: Structure problems
bullets: Order tasks by prerequisites: topological sort.
Cheapest edges linking all nodes: minimum spanning tree.
Track groups as they merge: union-find.

cards.title: Running times
cards.code:
BFS, DFS (list)     O(V + E)
BFS (matrix)        O(V²)
Dijkstra (heap)     O((V + E) log V)
Bellman-Ford        O(V × E)
Kruskal             O(E log E)
Prim (heap)         O(E log V)
Topological sort    O(V + E)
Edge check, matrix  O(1)

cards.title: When no fast way exists
cards.body: Some graph problems have no known fast exact method. The traveling salesperson problem asks for the shortest tour that visits every city once. Trying every possible order of n cities means about n! tours: 10 cities already give 3,628,800. Problems like this are called NP-complete.

cards.title: Good enough, fast
cards.body: A greedy approximation: always go to the closest city not visited yet. O(n²) time, O(n) space. Usually short, not always the shortest.

cards.title: How memory works
cards.body: Memory is a long row of numbered slots, and each slot's number is its address. An array keeps its items in one unbroken block, side by side (contiguous). So item i lives at the start address plus i times the item size, and reading any index is one jump: O(1). That is called random access.

cards.title: When an array fills
cards.body: The slot right after an array may already hold other data. To grow, the array must move: find a bigger free block and copy every item there, O(n). Dynamic arrays such as Python's list reserve spare slots and grow by a factor, so append averages O(1) (amortized), at the cost of some unused memory.

cards.title: Linked lists
cards.body: Nodes can sit anywhere in memory. Each holds a value and a link to the next node; the list keeps the head. Reaching item i means following i links from the head, O(n): sequential access.

cards.title: Insert and delete
cards.body: In a linked list you add or remove next to a node you already hold by changing one or two links, O(1). To push at the front: link the new node to the old head first, then make it the head (the other order loses the list). To drop the node after prev, point prev's link at the node after it. An array has to shift every later item instead, O(n).

cards.title: The cost table
cards.code:
array  linked list
read item i   O(1)   O(n)
insert front  O(n)   O(1)
insert middle O(n)   O(1)*
delete middle O(n)   O(1)*
search value  O(n)   O(n)
* once you hold the node before it

cards.title: Last in, first out
cards.body: A stack lets you touch only its top. Push puts an item on top and pop takes the top item off, so the newest item always leaves first (LIFO), like a pile of plates. Both are O(1). Undo history works this way: the latest action is undone first.

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
s = []
s.append('a')   # push
s.append('b')
print(s.pop())  # b
print(s[-1])    # a, the new top
cards.body: Use a list with its right end as the top. Lists have no push method; append is the push. pop(0) would take from the bottom and costs O(n).

cards.title: Matching brackets
cards.body: Read the text left to right and push every opening bracket. At a closing one the stack must not be empty; pop its partner. At the end the stack must be empty, or some opener was never closed. One pass: O(n) time, and up to O(n) space for the stack.

cards.title: The call stack
cards.code:
def inner():
    print('inner runs')
def outer():
    x = 1
    inner()  # outer waits here
    print('back in outer', x)
outer()
cards.body: Each call gets a frame on the call stack with its local variables. While inner runs, outer is paused with x kept; when inner returns, its frame is popped and outer carries on.

cards.title: Too deep
cards.body: Recursion pushes one frame per call, so depth n costs O(n) memory. A function that never reaches a base case keeps pushing until Python stops it with RecursionError (the default limit is 1,000 frames). The fix is a base case, or a loop instead.

cards.title: First in, first out
cards.body: A queue serves items in arrival order: enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front (FIFO), like a line at a bakery. Print jobs and breadth-first search use queues. Both operations should cost O(1).

cards.title: Use a deque
cards.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque()
q.append('x')       # enqueue
q.append('y')
print(q.popleft())  # x
cards.body: list.pop(0) shifts every remaining item, O(n). A deque (double-ended queue) is built for fast work at both ends.

cards.title: Both ends
bullets: append and pop work on the right end, O(1).
appendleft and popleft work on the left end, O(1).
Reading the middle of a deque by index is slower than in a list.
A list is only fast at its right end: insert(0, x) is O(n).

cards.title: Hash functions
cards.body: A hash function turns a key into a number. It must be consistent: the same key always gives the same number, or you could never find what you stored. A good one also spreads different keys evenly over the slots, so few of them share one.

cards.title: Array plus hash
cards.body: % folds any hash into a valid bucket index.

cards.title: Handling collisions
cards.body: Two different keys can land in the same bucket: a collision. Chaining keeps a small list in each bucket, as above; open addressing probes for another free slot. A few collisions are normal. If every key lands in one bucket, each lookup scans one long list, no better than a linked list.

cards.title: Load factor
cards.body: Load factor = items ÷ buckets. As it rises, so do collisions. A common rule: once it passes about 0.7, make an array twice as big and re-insert every item, O(n). Since the size doubles, resizes are rare, so inserts still average O(1) (amortized).

cards.title: What it costs
cards.code:
average  worst
lookup  O(1)     O(n)
insert  O(1)     O(n)
delete  O(1)     O(n)
cards.body: The worst case comes from keys piling into one bucket. A good hash function and a low load factor keep you at the average. Space is O(n).

cards.title: Dicts and sets
cards.code:
codes = {'France': 33, 'Japan': 81}
print(codes['Japan'])     # 81
print(codes.get('Peru'))  # None
print('Japan' in codes)   # True
cards.body: A dict is a hash table from keys to values; a set stores keys only. Lookups, inserts, deletes and in checks are O(1) on average. The same check on a list scans it, O(n).

cards.title: Catching repeats
cards.body: Keep everything you've seen in a set and test each new item against it before adding it. A whole stream of n items costs O(n) time and O(n) space. Doing the same test against a list rescans it every time, O(n²) in total. set(items) also drops duplicates in one go, without keeping order.

cards.title: Caching slow answers
cards.body: A cache remembers answers that were slow to get, keyed by the request. Look in the cache first. On a hit, return the saved answer. On a miss, do the slow work, save the result under its key, then return it. Repeat requests now cost one O(1) lookup. The cache itself must live outside the function, or it is lost after each call.

cards.title: Tree words
cards.body: A tree starts at one root node, and each node links down to its children. In a binary tree every node has at most two children, left and right. A node with no children is a leaf. The height is the number of levels on the longest path from the root down.

cards.title: The BST rule
cards.body: In a binary search tree, all keys in a node's left subtree are smaller than the node's key, and all keys in its right subtree are larger. To search, compare with the node and go left or right, ignoring the whole other side, much like binary search. To insert, follow the same path and attach the new node where it falls off (at None).

cards.title: Search in Python
cards.body: A recursive insert returns each subtree's root, so the parent relinks it: node.left = insert(node.left, key).

cards.title: Balance matters
cards.body: Search and insert cost O(h) for height h. A balanced tree has h about log₂ n, so O(log n). Insert keys in sorted order into a plain BST and each one goes right: a chain of height n, as slow as a linked list, O(n). Self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees rearrange nodes to keep h at O(log n).

cards.title: BST vs sorted array
bullets: Both find a key in O(log n) (the BST when balanced).
Sorted array: a new key means shifting items, O(n).
Balanced BST: a new key is linked in, O(log n).
Only the array can fetch item i in O(1); a BST has no index.
Databases use B-trees: wide balanced trees with many keys per node.

cards.title: Depth-first orders
bullets: Preorder: the node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree.
Inorder: left subtree, the node, right subtree.
Postorder: left subtree, right subtree, the node.
Inorder on a BST lists the keys in sorted order.

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: Move the print line between or after the two calls to get inorder or postorder.

cards.title: Level order
cards.body: Level order is breadth-first: row by row from the root, left to right inside each row. Use a queue: take a node from the front, then add its left and right children to the back.

cards.title: What it costs
cards.body: Every traversal visits each node once: O(n) time. The recursive ones use O(h) stack space for height h. Level order's queue can hold a whole row, so O(n) space in the worst case.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: A min-heap is a binary tree where every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the smallest item is always at the root. It is not fully sorted; it only promises the top. Heaps power priority queues: always handle the most urgent item next.

cards.title: Stored in a list
cards.body: A heap fills its tree row by row, so it fits in a plain list with no links. With the root at index 0, the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent is at (i − 1) // 2.

cards.title: heapq in Python
cards.code:
import heapq
h = []
for x in [7, 2, 9, 4]:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
print(h[0])              # 2, peek
print(heapq.heappop(h))  # 2
print(heapq.heappop(h))  # 4
cards.body: The heap list is the first argument. h.pop() would only remove the last list slot, not the smallest item.

cards.title: Keeping the top k
cards.body: To keep the k largest numbers of a stream, push each one into a min-heap and pop once it holds more than k. The smallest of the current best k sits on top, ready to be thrown out. That costs O(n log k) time and O(k) space, cheaper than sorting everything when k is small.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: push and pop: O(log n), along one root-to-leaf path.
Peek at h[0]: O(1).
heapq.heapify on a list: O(n).
No extra space beyond the list itself.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: A trie (prefix tree) stores words letter by letter. Each node maps a character to a child node, a word is a path down from the root, and a flag marks the nodes where a word ends. Words that start the same share their first nodes.

cards.title: Lookup in Python
cards.body: Insert walks the same way, creating a child whenever a letter is missing, then sets is_end.

cards.title: What it costs
cards.body: Inserting or looking up a word of length L is O(L) whatever the number of stored words, since each dict step is O(1) on average. Insert adds at most L nodes. To list all words with a prefix, walk the prefix once and explore below it, which is why tries suit autocomplete.

cards.title: Pick the structure
bullets: Newest first: stack.
Oldest first, in arrival order: queue.
Most urgent first: heap.
Is it here? What is its value? Hash set or dict.
Everything sharing a prefix: trie.

cards.title: Huge sets, little memory
cards.body: Some sets are enormous, such as every URL a web crawler has seen, and a hash set of all of them takes a lot of memory. Probabilistic structures give up a little accuracy to use a tiny fraction of that space.

cards.title: Bloom filter
cards.body: A bloom filter is a bit array plus k hash functions, and it stores no items. To add an item, set the k bits its hashes point to. To check one, read those k bits: any 0 means it was never added; all 1s means it was probably added, since other items may have set the same bits.

cards.title: In Python
Maybe yes, never wrong no
bullets: False positives can happen.
False negatives can't: an added item's bits stay 1.
Items can't be removed: clearing a bit could erase others too.
Add and check cost O(k) time; memory is just the bits.

cards.title: Counting with HyperLogLog
cards.body: HyperLogLog estimates how many distinct items a huge stream holds, like unique visitors, without storing them. It hashes each item and keeps only small summaries of the hash patterns; a long run of leading zero bits is rare, so seeing one hints that many items went by. Memory stays small and fixed; the count is close, not exact.

cards.title: Which one when
bullets: Exact answers and it fits in memory: hash set.
Is it in a giant set, rare false yes is fine: bloom filter.
About how many distinct items: HyperLogLog.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it. Each call does a little of the work and hands the rest to the next call, until the input is so small that the answer is obvious.

cards.title: Two parts
bullets: Base case: answered directly, with no further call
Recursive case: the function calls itself on a smaller input
Every recursive call must move toward the base case
No base case, or a step away from it, and the calls never stop

cards.title: An example
cards.code:
def stars(n):
    if n == 0:        # base case
        print("done")
        return
    print("*" * n)
    stars(n - 1)      # smaller

stars(3)
# ***
# **
# *
# done

cards.title: Recursion or loop?
cards.body: Anything written with recursion can be written with a loop, sometimes with your own stack to remember unfinished work. Recursion is picked because the code reads more clearly, not for speed. In Python each call costs a stack frame, so a loop is often faster and safer for simple repetition.

cards.title: Paused calls
cards.body: When a function calls another, the caller pauses part way through. Python keeps its arguments and local variables in a frame and pushes that frame on the call stack. When a call returns, its frame is popped and the caller carries on where it stopped.

cards.title: Last in, first out
A frame per call
cards.body: Each frame has its own copy of the variables, so n in one call never clashes with n in another. Calling sum_to(n) makes n + 1 calls, and at the deepest point all of them are waiting: O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

cards.title: Too deep
cards.body: Every waiting call takes memory. Python caps the depth (1,000 by default, see sys.getrecursionlimit()) and raises RecursionError when a chain of calls grows past it, for example when a function has no base case.

cards.title: Depth vs total calls
cards.body: The stack only holds the calls that are waiting right now: one path from the first call down to a base case. A function can make a huge number of calls in total while its stack stays shallow, because finished calls are popped off.

cards.title: The recipe
bullets: Find the simplest input: that is the base case
Shrink or split the problem until you reach it
Combine the answers on the way back up
For lists the base case is usually an empty or one-item list

cards.title: A product, recursively
cards.body: The base case returns the value that leaves the answer unchanged: 1 for a product, 0 for a sum. Each call handles one item and trusts the call below for the rest.

cards.title: Combining answers
cards.body: To find the largest item, compare the current item with the largest of the rest, which the recursive call hands back; a one-item list is its own answer. Trees split in two: an empty tree is the base case, a tree's size is 1 + left size + right size, and its height is 1 + the max of the two heights.

cards.title: Euclid's method
cards.body: The greatest common divisor shrinks the pair on every call: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b), and gcd(a, 0) = a. The numbers at least halve every two steps, so it takes O(log min(a, b)) calls.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: One call per item: O(n) time, O(n) stack
Halving each call: O(log n) depth
Slicing a[1:] copies the list: O(n²) time; pass an index instead

cards.title: Choose, explore, undo
cards.body: Backtracking builds an answer one choice at a time. Make a choice, recurse to handle everything that follows from it, then undo the choice (often with list.pop()) so the next option starts from a clean slate.

cards.title: An example
cards.code:
def strings(n, cur, out):
    if len(cur) == n:
        out.append("".join(cur))
        return
    for ch in "ab":
        cur.append(ch)
        strings(n, cur, out)
        cur.pop()     # undo

out = []
strings(2, [], out)
print(out)
# ['aa', 'ab', 'ba', 'bb']

cards.title: Prune early
cards.body: If a partial answer already breaks a rule, skip it, and nothing built on top of it is ever explored. In N-Queens a square attacked by an earlier queen is never tried. That cuts the search a lot, though the worst case still grows like n!.

cards.title: How many answers
bullets: Subsets of n items: 2ⁿ, each item in or out
Orderings of n items: n!
Time grows with the number of answers times their size
Stack depth is one level per choice: O(n)

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: A greedy algorithm builds its answer step by step and always takes the choice that looks best right now, without ever going back. That makes it simple and fast, but it only finds the true best answer for some problems.

cards.title: Scheduling works
cards.body: To fit the most talks into one room, sort them by end time and keep each talk that starts once the last kept one has ended. Ending early leaves the most room for the rest, and this rule is proven optimal. O(n log n) for the sort, then one pass.
cards.code:
talks (start, end), by end:
(1,3) keep    (2,5) skip
(4,6) keep    (6,8) keep
(5,9) skip

cards.title: When greedy fails
cards.body: Taking the biggest thing first can backfire. Coins 1, 4 and 5 for amount 8: greedy pays 5 + 1 + 1 + 1, but 4 + 4 uses two coins. An 8 kg bag: grabbing a 6 kg item worth $50 blocks two 4 kg items worth $30 each ($60). Whole items like these need dynamic programming for the exact answer.

cards.title: Fractions allowed
cards.body: If you may take part of an item, like spices sold by weight, greedy is optimal: take the item with the highest value per kg first, as much as fits, then the next best. This is the fractional knapsack: O(n log n) to sort by value per kg.

cards.title: Good enough answers
cards.body: For hard problems with no fast exact method, greedy gives a quick approximation. Set cover: to cover every needed skill with few people, keep adding the person who brings the most skills not covered yet. Touring many stops: always go to the nearest unvisited one next.

cards.title: Repeated work
cards.body: Naive Fibonacci calls fib(n − 1) and fib(n − 2), and each of those branches again, so small inputs are solved over and over. If calls(n) counts the calls, then calls(n) = 1 + calls(n − 1) + calls(n − 2), with 1 call for n < 2: fib(4) makes 9 calls, and the total grows like 2ⁿ.

cards.title: Save each answer
Let Python cache
cards.body: functools.cache, or lru_cache(maxsize=None), wraps a function and stores its results for you. With each input solved only once, Fibonacci drops from O(2ⁿ) to O(n) time, using O(n) space for the cache and the stack.

cards.title: Split on the last move
cards.body: Counting problems often split on the final step. If you may climb 1 or 3 stairs at a time, every climb of n ends with a 1-step (after n − 1) or a 3-step (after n − 3), so ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 3).

cards.title: DP words
bullets: Overlapping subproblems: the same smaller problem keeps coming up
Optimal substructure: the best answer is built from best answers to parts
Memoization: top-down recursion that saves answers
Tabulation: a bottom-up loop that fills a table
Backtracking (not DP): try a choice, recurse, undo it

cards.title: Bottom-up tables
cards.body: Tabulation drops the recursion: make a list, set the base cases, then fill the rest in order so each entry only uses entries already filled. No recursive calls means no recursion limit.
cards.code:
def ways(n):  # steps of 1 or 3
    dp = [1] + [0] * n
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1]
        if i >= 3:
            dp[i] += dp[i - 3]
    return dp[n]

print(ways(5))   # 4

cards.title: Fewest coins
cards.body: dp[a] holds the fewest coins for amount a. dp[0] is 0 and every other amount starts at infinity (not reachable yet). For each coin c and each amount a from c up, paying with c costs dp[a − c] + 1; keep the smaller value. O(amount × coins) time, O(amount) space.

cards.title: Counting combinations
cards.body: To count the ways instead, start with dp[0] = 1 (one way to make 0: no coins) and add dp[a − c] into dp[a]. With the coin loop outside, coins join one at a time, so 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 count once. With the loops swapped you count orderings instead.

cards.title: Keep only what you need
cards.body: House robber: for each house, either skip it and keep the best total so far, or take it and add its value to the best total that ended two houses back. Only the last two results matter, so two variables replace the table: O(n) time, O(1) space.

cards.title: Increasing subsequence
cards.body: For the longest increasing subsequence, dp[i] is the longest one ending at nums[i]. Start each entry at 1, the item alone. For every earlier j with a smaller value, nums[i] can extend that run by one more. Two nested loops: O(n²) time, O(n) space.

cards.title: The problem
cards.body: 0/1 knapsack: each item has a weight and a value, you take an item whole or not at all, and the bag has a weight limit W. Trying every set of items is O(2ⁿ), and greedy can miss the best set. Dynamic programming finds it exactly.

cards.title: The grid
cards.body: Make one row per item and one column per capacity from 0 to W. A cell holds the best value using only the items up to that row, in a bag of that capacity. Adding a row never lowers a value, and the bottom-right cell is the answer. O(n × W) time and space.

cards.title: Filling one cell
cards.body: For an item of weight w and value v at capacity c: skip it and copy the cell above, or, if it fits, take it and add v to the row above at capacity c − w. Keep the larger.
cards.code:
item 2 kg, $30; capacity 5
skip: cell above     = $45
take: 30 + (row above,
      capacity 3: $25) = $55
cell = max(45, 55)   = $55

cards.title: One row is enough
cards.body: A single row dp[cap] also works. Loop capacity from high to low, so dp[cap − w] still holds the value from before this item and the item is used at most once. Low to high would let an item be reused (the unbounded knapsack). Space drops to O(W).

cards.title: Where it breaks
bullets: Weights must match the grid's steps: a 0.5 kg item needs half-kg columns
Items that change each other's cost break it: subproblems must be independent
Part of an item allowed? Greedy by value per kg is simpler and exact

cards.title: Substring or subsequence
cards.body: A substring is a run of letters side by side: "ell" in "hello". A subsequence keeps the order but may skip letters: "hlo" in "hello". The longest common substring rewards one unbroken match; the longest common subsequence counts letters that match in order, gaps allowed.

cards.title: Substring grid
cards.body: One word down the side, the other across the top. On a match a cell is 1 + the cell up and to the left; on a mismatch it is 0, because the run is broken. So the answer is the largest number anywhere in the grid, not always the last cell.

cards.title: Subsequence grid
cards.body: Same grid, one change: on a mismatch take the larger of the cell above and the cell to the left, since skipping a letter of either word is allowed. Matches still add 1 to the diagonal. Values never drop, so the last cell holds the answer. Both grids take O(m × n) time and space.

cards.title: Padding in code
cards.code:
def grid(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1)
          for _ in range(m + 1)]
    # row 0 and column 0 stay 0
    # (empty prefixes), so cell
    # (i, j) compares a[i-1]
    # with b[j-1]
    return dp

cards.title: Edit distance and uses
cards.body: Edit distance (Levenshtein) is the fewest single-letter inserts, deletes and replacements that turn one word into another. On a match a cell copies the diagonal; otherwise it is 1 + the smallest of its three neighbours. Grids like these drive spell checkers, diff tools and DNA comparison.

cards.title: Names that explain
cards.body: A good name tells the reader what a thing holds or does, so nobody has to open the body to find out. Use verbs for functions (send_invoice, count_words) and nouns for data. Vague names like data, process or do_it, and cryptic short codes, make everyone guess.

cards.title: PEP 8 naming
bullets: lower_case_with_underscores: variables and functions
CapWords: classes, e.g. OrderLine
ALL_CAPS: constants, e.g. PAGE_SIZE
Leading underscore, e.g. _helper: internal detail. It is only a convention; Python does not block access.

cards.title: No magic numbers
cards.body: A bare number in the middle of code is a magic number: the reader has to guess what it means. Give it a name in capitals. The name explains it, and if the value changes there is one line to edit.
cards.code:
SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400

def to_seconds(days):
    return days * SECONDS_PER_DAY

print(to_seconds(2))  # 172800

cards.title: DRY, KISS, YAGNI
bullets: DRY, Don't Repeat Yourself: each piece of logic lives in one place, so a fix is made once
KISS, Keep It Simple: choose the simplest design that works
YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It: don't build a feature before it is needed
Single responsibility: each module or function has one reason to change

cards.title: One job per function
cards.body: Split a long function into small steps that each do one job. Each step gets a clear name, can be tested with a few cases and reused elsewhere. This is for people, not speed: it does not make Python run faster or use less memory, and it cannot promise zero bugs.

sources.title: PEP 8: Style Guide for Python Code

cards.title: What pure means
cards.body: A pure function's result depends only on its arguments, and it changes nothing outside itself: no global variables, no printing, no editing its inputs. Same input, same output, every time. That makes it easy to test, safe to reuse and safe to cache.

cards.title: Hidden state hurts
cards.body: bump depends on and changes a global, so the same argument gives a different answer each call. Every test must set up and reset that hidden value. A pure add(a, b) needs nothing but its arguments.
cards.code:
count = 0

def bump(n):
    global count
    count += n
    return count

print(bump(1), bump(1))  # 1 2

cards.title: Don't edit your inputs
cards.body: A function receives the caller's actual list, not a copy, so tags.append(t) would change it behind their back. Returning a new list keeps the function pure. Copying costs O(n) time and O(n) space, which is usually worth it.
cards.code:
def with_tag(tags, t):
    return tags + [t]

mine = ["a"]
new = with_tag(mine, "b")
print(mine, new)
# ['a'] ['a', 'b']

cards.title: Bonus: caching
cards.body: A pure function always gives the same answer for the same input, so its results can be stored. functools.cache (or lru_cache, which can cap the size) remembers each result. Plain recursive Fibonacci takes exponential time, about O(2^n); cached, each n is computed once: O(n) time, O(n) space.

cards.title: Guard clauses
cards.body: Handle the odd or invalid cases first and return early. The main path then sits flat at the left margin, with no else branch and no deep nesting. The gain is readability, not speed.

cards.title: Raise at the source
cards.body: When a bad value arrives, raise a specific exception right there. The caller gets a clear message and a precise type to catch. Returning None or carrying on lets the bad value travel and fail somewhere harder to trace.

cards.title: Ask forgiveness (EAFP)
cards.body: EAFP means: easier to ask forgiveness than permission. Just try the action, and handle the one failure you planned for in except.

cards.title: Know the exception
bullets: int("abc") raises ValueError
A missing dict key raises KeyError
A list index past the end raises IndexError
KeyError and IndexError are both kinds of LookupError
A misspelled name raises NameError

cards.title: Avoid bare except
cards.body: A bare except: is legal Python, but it catches everything: a NameError from a typo, even KeyboardInterrupt from Ctrl+C. Real bugs then silently become a default value. Catch only the exception you expect, so every other bug still shows up.

cards.title: Pick by the job
bullets: list: ordered, index O(1), search with in O(n)
dict: look up a value by key, O(1) on average
set: unique items, in is O(1) on average
deque: add or remove at either end in O(1)
tuple: a fixed record that should not change

cards.title: Queues need a deque
cards.body: For first-in, first-out work, add at the back and take from the front. list.pop(0) shifts every remaining item left, O(n) per call. deque.popleft() is O(1).
cards.code:
from collections import deque

line = deque()
line.append("a")
line.append("b")
print(line.popleft())  # a

cards.title: Look up by key
cards.body: Searching a list of records for one id scans it: O(n) per lookup. Build a dict once, O(n) time and O(n) space, and each lookup after that is O(1) on average. For many lookups the dict wins easily.
cards.code:
users = [(7, "Ann"), (9, "Bo")]
by_id = dict(users)
print(by_id[9])  # Bo

cards.title: Mutable default trap
cards.body: A default value is created once, when def runs, not on every call. A default list is shared by all calls and keeps growing. Default to None and make the list inside.
cards.code:
def collect(x, into=None):
    if into is None:
        into = []
    into.append(x)
    return into

print(collect(1), collect(2))
# [1] [2]

cards.title: Type hints
cards.body: Hints say what goes in and what comes out: name: type for a parameter and -> type for the return value. Python does not enforce them when the code runs; editors and checkers such as mypy use them to catch mistakes early.

cards.title: What dataclasses do
cards.body: @dataclass reads the annotated fields and writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you. Fields with a default must come after fields without one, the same rule as function parameters; otherwise you get a TypeError. This prints Book(title='Dune', pages=100).

cards.title: Frozen dataclasses
cards.body: frozen=True makes instances read-only: assigning to a field raises FrozenInstanceError. Read-only values are safe to share, and a frozen dataclass is hashable by default, so it can be a dict key or a set member.

cards.title: Mutable field defaults
cards.body: A dataclass rejects a field written as tags: list = [] with a ValueError, because one list would be shared. Give field() a default_factory instead: a function called once per new instance, so each gets a fresh value.
cards.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from dataclasses import field

@dataclass
class Team:
    scores: dict = field(
        default_factory=dict)

print(Team())  # Team(scores={})

cards.title: Optional properties
cards.body: A ? after a property name means the property may be missing. Its type then also includes undefined, so here nickname is string | undefined.

cards.title: any versus unknown
cards.body: any switches type checking off: you can do anything with the value, including mistakes. unknown also accepts any value, but you must narrow it with a check such as typeof before using it.

cards.title: Generic functions
cards.body: A type parameter in angle brackets, often called T, lets one function work for any element type while keeping the exact type. last([1, 2]) returns a number; last(["a"]) returns a string.

cards.title: Discriminated unions
cards.body: A union of object types that share a field with literal values, like done below, is a discriminated union. Checking that field tells the compiler which shape you have, so it can make sure every case is handled.

cards.title: Single responsibility
cards.body: A class should have one reason to change. One that fetches prices, builds a web page and saves backups has three, and a change to one job can break the others. Split it into small classes, each easy to test.

cards.title: Open/closed principle
cards.body: Open for extension, closed for modification. An if/elif chain on a kind field must be reopened for every new case. Give each class its own method instead: a new case is a new class, and the calling loop never changes.

cards.title: L, I and D
bullets: Liskov substitution: a subclass must work anywhere its parent is expected
Interface segregation: several small interfaces beat one giant one
Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete classes
SOLID are guides, not laws: reach for them when code is hard to change or test

cards.title: Has-a beats is-a
cards.body: Inheritance says is-a: a Square is a Shape. Composition says has-a: an object keeps another in an attribute and hands work to it. A phone has a battery, so it holds one, and a different or fake battery can be passed in without touching Phone.

cards.title: Tests with assert
cards.body: A test calls code with a known input and checks the result with assert, which raises AssertionError when the condition is false. Runners such as pytest find functions whose names start with test_ and run them all.

cards.title: Dependency injection
cards.body: Pass a function's or class's collaborators in (database, clock, mailer) instead of creating them inside. The caller chooses: real code passes the real thing, a test passes a stand-in. This prints 42 hi.
cards.code:
import time

def stamp(msg, now=time.time):
    return f"{now():.0f} {msg}"

print(stamp("hi", now=lambda: 42))

cards.title: Inject through __init__
cards.body: Alarm is handed a clock and only cares that it can call it. Writing self.clock = time.time inside __init__ would tie the class to the real clock for good.

cards.title: Fakes record calls
cards.body: A fake has the same methods as the real object but only records what it was asked to do, so no message is really sent. A test has three steps: arrange (build the fake and the object), act (call the method), assert (check what the fake saw).

cards.title: Clients and services
cards.body: A service is a program on a server that waits on a known port for requests, such as DNS on port 53. A client sends its request to the server's IP address and that port. Services like DHCP, DNS and NTP are what let ordinary hosts join a network and use it.

cards.title: Four IPv4 settings
bullets: Its own IP address.
Its subnet mask, to tell local addresses from remote ones.
A default gateway: a router inside its own subnet.
One or more DNS server addresses (two, for backup).

cards.title: Static or DHCP
cards.body: Routers, servers and printers usually get fixed (static) addresses so others can find them. User devices usually learn all four settings from DHCP. Either way, the gateway must sit inside the host's own subnet; with a /24 mask, that means the first three octets of host and gateway must match.

cards.title: When one is wrong
bullets: Wrong address or mask: local hosts look remote, or remote ones look local.
Gateway outside the subnet or wrong: the local subnet works, every other subnet fails.
Bad DNS server: pinging an IP address works, but names do not resolve.

cards.title: Seeing the settings
cards.code:
ipconfig /all     Windows
ip address        Linux
ip route          Linux
ifconfig          macOS, Linux
netstat -rn       macOS, Linux

cards.title: Why DHCP
cards.body: DHCP gives a host all four settings automatically: its address and mask, the gateway, and DNS servers. Addresses are leased for a set time, so the server can reuse addresses of devices that leave. It avoids typing mistakes and lets a laptop join any network. DHCP runs over UDP: servers listen on port 67, clients on 68.

cards.title: The DORA exchange
bullets: Discover: the client broadcasts, looking for any server.
Offer: a server offers an address and settings.
Request: the client asks for the offered address.
Acknowledge: the server confirms, and the lease starts.

cards.title: No address yet
cards.body: While it asks, the client has no IP address, so it sends from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255, which reaches every host on this LAN only. Routers never forward that broadcast. The server's replies may be broadcast too; the client spots its own by the client ID (its MAC address) inside.

cards.title: DHCP relay
cards.body: A central server can't hear broadcasts from other subnets. So the router on each LAN acts as a relay agent: it catches DHCP broadcasts and forwards them as unicasts to the server's address (on Cisco, the ip helper-address command), then passes the replies back onto the LAN.

cards.title: Leases and renewal
cards.body: The server keeps an address pool per subnet, skips excluded addresses kept for static use, and sets the lease time. By default the client asks its server to renew halfway through the lease (T1, 50%), and asks any server at 87.5% (T2). A 24-hour lease taken at 06:00 is first renewed at 18:00.

cards.title: When DHCP fails
cards.body: If no server answers, many systems give themselves a link-local (APIPA) address from 169.254.0.0/16. It comes with no gateway or DNS, so the host can only reach other 169.254 hosts on the same link. Seeing one means: check the path to the DHCP server.
