cards.title: Names to numbers
cards.body: People type names; packets need IP addresses. DNS turns a name like www.example.com into an address before the real connection starts. A host asks the DNS server it learned from DHCP or its settings. Queries use port 53, usually over UDP; TCP is used for large answers and zone transfers.

cards.title: A tree of names
cards.body: Read a name right to left: the root, then a top-level domain such as com, then example, then www. No server knows every name. Root servers point to the TLD servers, which point to each domain's authoritative servers, which hold the actual records.

cards.title: Resolving a name
cards.body: The host hands the whole job to its resolver (a recursive query). The resolver walks down the tree with iterative queries: each server answers or points it one level lower.
cards.code:
host -> resolver: www.example.com?
resolver -> root:  try .com
resolver -> .com:  try example.com
resolver -> example.com:
                   192.0.2.80
resolver -> host:  192.0.2.80

cards.title: Caching and TTL
cards.body: Resolvers and hosts cache answers. Each record carries a TTL in seconds, and until it runs out, repeat lookups are answered from the cache with no trip up the tree. That is why a changed record can take a while to show up everywhere.

cards.title: Record types
bullets: A: name to IPv4 address.
AAAA: name to IPv6 address.
CNAME: an alias that points to another name.
MX: the mail server for a domain.
NS: an authoritative server for a zone. PTR: an address back to its name (reverse lookup).

cards.title: Why NAT
cards.body: Private addresses (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) are not routed on the Internet. NAT, on the edge router or firewall, rewrites them to public addresses on the way out and back again on the way in. Thousands of private hosts can share a few public addresses, which helped IPv4 last.

cards.title: Cisco's address names
bullets: Inside local: the inside host's real, usually private, address.
Inside global: the public address that stands for it outside.
Outside global: the outside host's real address.
Outside local: how the outside host looks from inside (usually the same).

cards.title: Three kinds
bullets: Static NAT: one private address always maps to the same public one, so outside hosts can start connections to it.
Dynamic NAT: private hosts borrow public addresses from a pool, one each.
PAT (overload): many hosts share one public address, told apart by port number.

cards.title: A PAT table
cards.body: Going out, the router swaps the source address and port for its public address and a free port, and records the pair. Coming back, it looks up the destination port of the reply, swaps back, and forwards the packet onto the LAN.

cards.title: Costs and limits
cards.body: Kept in a hash map keyed by address and port, a lookup is O(1) on average, and the table needs O(n) memory for n active flows. One public address has about 65,000 ports to hand out. Outside hosts cannot start a connection to a PAT host unless a static mapping is added.

cards.title: Why time matters
cards.body: Every router, switch and server keeps its own clock. If the clocks disagree, log messages from different devices can't be lined up when you trace a problem, and time checks such as certificate expiry can fail. NTP keeps all the clocks close to one good source.

cards.title: How it works
cards.body: An NTP client asks one or more servers for the time over UDP port 123. It measures the round-trip delay, corrects for it and adjusts its clock gradually. A device can be a client and a server at once, passing time on down the line.

cards.title: Stratum levels
bullets: Stratum 1: a server fed directly by a reference clock such as GPS.
Each hop away adds 1: a client of stratum 1 is stratum 2, and so on.
Lower stratum means closer to the reference clock.
Stratum 16 means not synchronized.

cards.title: Good practice
bullets: Point each device at two or more NTP servers.
Let a few core devices sync from outside and serve the rest of the network.
Turn on NTP authentication so a fake server can't shift your clocks.

cards.title: Three ways in
bullets: Console: a cable into the device's console port. Works with no IP set up at all.
Telnet: the command line over the network, TCP port 23.
SSH: the command line over the network, TCP port 22.

cards.title: Why not Telnet
cards.body: Telnet sends everything as clear text, user name and password included, so anyone who captures the traffic can read them. SSH encrypts the whole session and proves the server's identity with its key, so it has replaced Telnet for managing devices.

cards.title: SSH on Cisco
cards.body: A Cisco switch names its RSA key from its hostname plus domain name, so both must be set before the key can be made. SSH logins need a user name.
cards.code:
hostname EDGE2
ip domain name lab.test
crypto key generate rsa
username ops secret ********
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input ssh

cards.title: Remote needs IP
cards.body: Telnet and SSH ride the IP network, so the device needs an IP address (on a switch, on a VLAN interface) and a default gateway to be reached from other subnets. The console needs neither, which makes it the way in on day one or after a bad change.

cards.title: SNMP roles
cards.body: An SNMP manager (monitoring software) watches many devices. Each device runs an SNMP agent that keeps values such as interface counters and CPU load in its MIB. The manager reads them with Get and changes them with Set, and the agent can warn the manager on its own with a Trap or Inform.

cards.title: Ports and versions
bullets: The manager polls agents on UDP 161.
Agents send traps to the manager on UDP 162.
v1 and v2c: a community string acts as the password, sent in clear text.
v3: adds users, authentication and encryption.

cards.title: Syslog event messages
cards.body: Devices also write event messages: a link went down, a login failed. Syslog sends copies to a central server, usually over UDP 514, so you can search every device's logs in one place, with NTP keeping the time stamps in line. Each message has a severity from 0 to 7.

cards.title: Severity levels
cards.body: Lower number, more serious. Picking a level keeps that level and everything more serious: level 2 keeps 0, 1 and 2.
cards.code:
0  Emergency   unusable
1  Alert       act now
2  Critical
3  Error
4  Warning
5  Notice      normal but notable
6  Informational
7  Debug

cards.title: How FTP works
cards.body: FTP copies files after a login. The client opens a control connection to TCP port 21 and sends commands such as USER, PASS and RETR; the file itself travels on a separate data connection (from port 20 in classic active mode). FTP can list folders. Everything, password included, is clear text.

cards.title: How TFTP works
cards.body: TFTP is a tiny file copier on UDP port 69. No login and no folder listing: you name a file, and it comes in 512-byte blocks, each acknowledged before the next is sent. A file of n bytes takes about n/512 round trips: O(n) time, O(1) memory. Boot-time loaders like that simplicity.

cards.title: Side by side
cards.code:
FTP          TFTP
transport TCP 21 + 20  UDP 69
login     yes          no
list dir  yes          no
encrypted no           no

cards.title: Finding the server
cards.body: A device that boots with no settings needs to know which TFTP server to use. DHCP can include the TFTP server's address in the lease along with the IP settings; Cisco IP phones fetch their configuration files this way.

cards.title: Safer choices
bullets: SFTP: file transfer inside an SSH session (TCP 22).
FTPS: FTP protected with TLS.
Keep TFTP to trusted networks.

cards.title: Why layers
cards.body: Networking is split into layers so each part has one job. A layer uses the service of the layer below and serves the layer above. Across the network, matching layers talk to each other: the TCP code on one host reads the TCP header that the TCP code on the other host wrote.

cards.title: The five TCP/IP layers
bullets: 5 Application: what apps need, such as HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, POP3.
4 Transport: TCP or UDP, delivery between programs.
3 Network: IP addresses and routing over the whole path.
2 Data link: rules for one link, such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
1 Physical: cables, radio, signals and bits.

cards.title: OSI numbering
cards.body: The older OSI model has seven layers. Its bottom four match TCP/IP's in name and number. OSI splits the top into session (5), presentation (6) and application (7); TCP/IP folds all three into one application layer. People still use OSI numbers, so a web protocol is a 'Layer 7' protocol and IP is 'Layer 3'.

cards.title: Who does what
cards.body: On a laptop, the network card handles the physical and data-link layers, the operating system runs IP plus TCP and UDP, and apps such as a browser speak the application protocol. TCP/IP itself is defined in documents called RFCs.

sources.title: CCNA 200-301 Official Cert Guide (Odom et al., 2025), Vol. 1 ch. 1

cards.title: Wrapping data
cards.body: When a host sends, each layer puts its own header in front of what the layer above handed down. The data-link layer also adds a trailer at the end. This wrapping is encapsulation. The receiver peels the layers off in reverse order, which is de-encapsulation.

cards.title: Sending, layer by layer
cards.code:
app data      page
+ TCP header  TCP|page
+ IP header   IP|TCP|page
+ frame       Eth|IP|TCP|page|FCS
bits          0110 1001 ...

cards.title: Names for each unit
bullets: Segment: a TCP header plus its data (transport).
Packet: an IP header plus its data (network).
Frame: link header, packet and link trailer (data link).
PDU: the general word for any of these.

cards.title: At every router
cards.body: A router checks the arriving frame, throws away its link header and trailer, picks the next hop for the packet, then wraps the packet in a fresh frame for the next link. So the MAC addresses change on every hop, while the source and destination IP addresses stay the same end to end (NAT is the exception).

cards.title: The Ethernet frame
bullets: Destination MAC (6 bytes): who should get it.
Source MAC (6 bytes): who sent it.
Type (2 bytes): what is inside, such as IPv4 or IPv6.
Data: the packet, 46 to 1500 bytes (1500 is the MTU).
FCS (4 bytes, the trailer): an error check.

cards.title: MAC addresses
cards.body: A MAC address is 48 bits (6 bytes), written as 12 hex digits, such as 3c:52:a1:07:9e:44 (Cisco shows 3c52.a107.9e44). The first 3 bytes are the maker's OUI, assigned by the IEEE; the maker numbers the last 3 so each card is unique. Other names: hardware, physical or burned-in address.

cards.title: Who receives it
bullets: Unicast: one interface.
Broadcast, ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff: every device on the LAN.
Multicast: a group of devices that chose to listen.

cards.title: Catching errors
cards.body: The sender runs a math check over the frame and puts the result in the FCS. The receiver repeats the math. If the results differ, the frame was damaged and is simply dropped. Ethernet detects errors but never resends; TCP, higher up, notices the missing data and has it sent again.

cards.title: Finding a MAC: ARP
cards.body: To build a frame, a host needs the next device's MAC. ARP broadcasts a request like 'who has 192.168.3.9?' and that device replies with its MAC. Answers are kept in an ARP cache for a while, so ARP runs only now and then. On a PC, arp -a lists the cache.

cards.title: 32 bits, four octets
cards.body: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers from 0 to 255 with dots between them (dotted decimal), like 192.0.2.44. Each number is one octet, 8 bits. Every interface that sends or receives IP packets needs its own address.

cards.title: Network and host parts
cards.body: Addresses on one LAN share their first bits, the prefix (network part). The remaining bits, the host part, tell the hosts apart. A subnet mask marks the split: 1s over the prefix, 0s over the host bits. The 1s must all sit on the left, so a mask like 255.0.255.0 is illegal.

cards.title: Three mask formats
cards.body: A mask can be written in binary, in dotted decimal, or as a prefix: a slash and the count of 1 bits. /21 is 8 + 8 + 5 ones, so it is 255.255.248.0. Each mask octet can only be one of these values:

cards.title: Private ranges
cards.body: RFC 1918 sets these blocks aside for use inside any organization. Internet routers do not carry them, so NAT translates them at the edge.

cards.title: Old address classes
cards.body: Before CIDR, the first octet fixed the mask: Class A is 1-126 (/8), B is 128-191 (/16), C is 192-223 (/24). 224-239 is multicast (Class D). 127.x.x.x is loopback, a host talking to itself. Today any prefix length can be used.

cards.title: Counting addresses
cards.body: With H host bits a block holds 2**H addresses. The lowest names the network and the highest is its broadcast, so 2**H - 2 are usable. Python does the math in O(1):
cards.code:
import ipaddress
n = ipaddress.ip_network(
    '10.0.0.0/8')
print(n.netmask)  # 255.0.0.0
print(n.num_addresses - 2)
# 16777214

cards.title: What a subnet is
cards.body: A subnet is a run of consecutive addresses that share a prefix. With a /p mask the host part has 32 - p bits. The lowest address (host bits all 0) is the subnet ID. The highest (host bits all 1) is the subnet broadcast. Everything in between can go to hosts.

cards.title: The block size trick
cards.body: Find the octet where the mask is neither 255 nor 0. The block size is 256 minus that mask octet, and subnet IDs are multiples of it. The multiple at or below the address is the subnet ID; the next multiple minus 1 is the broadcast. If the mask is all 255s and 0s, use the octet just after the last 255.

cards.title: Check with Python
cards.body: The subnet ID is the address AND the mask, one bit operation: O(1) time and space. Listing every host is O(2**H).
cards.code:
import ipaddress
i = ipaddress.ip_interface(
    '198.51.100.150/26')
n = i.network
print(n)  # 198.51.100.128/26
print(n.broadcast_address)
print(n[1], n[-2])  # usable
print(len(list(n.hosts())))  # 62

cards.title: Same subnet or not
cards.body: Two addresses are in the same subnet only if they give the same subnet ID under the mask. Looking alike is not enough: with /27, .30 and .33 sit in different blocks (.0 and .32). Hosts in the same subnet talk directly; different subnets need a router between them.

cards.title: Local or remote
cards.body: Before sending, a host checks whether the destination is in its own subnet. If it is, the host sends the frame straight to that host. If not, it sends the frame to its default gateway (default router), a router on its own subnet, which carries the packet on.

cards.title: The routing table
cards.body: Each router keeps a table of subnets, each with an outgoing interface and often a next-hop router. Routes come from directly connected subnets, from static routes typed in by an admin, and from routing protocols such as OSPF, where routers tell each other what they can reach.

cards.title: Most specific wins
cards.body: If several routes match, the router uses the longest prefix. A default route, 0.0.0.0/0, matches everything, so it is used only when nothing else matches. Without one, an unmatched packet is dropped.

cards.title: Lookup in Python
cards.body: This scan checks all n routes: O(n) time and up to O(n) space per packet. Real routers use tries or special hardware to match faster.
cards.code:
import ipaddress as ip
t = {'172.16.0.0/16': 'R1',
     '172.16.8.0/22': 'R2',
     '0.0.0.0/0': 'R3'}
def route(dst):
    d = ip.ip_address(dst)
    hits = [ip.ip_network(r)
        for r in t
        if d in ip.ip_network(r)]
    best = max(hits,
        key=lambda n: n.prefixlen)
    return t[str(best)]
print(route('172.16.9.4'))  # R2

cards.title: Work at each hop
bullets: Check the FCS; drop the frame if damaged.
Peel off the incoming Ethernet wrapping; only the packet is kept.
Match the destination IP against the table.
Wrap the packet in a new frame and send it out the matched interface.

cards.title: ARP for the gateway
cards.body: When the destination is remote, the frame still needs a destination MAC, but it is the gateway's MAC, not the far host's. So the host runs ARP for its gateway's IP address. The far host's MAC is learned by the last router, which ARPs on the far LAN.

cards.title: Two transports
bullets: TCP: opens a connection, numbers each segment, acknowledges what arrives, resends what is lost, delivers in order.
UDP: just sends datagrams. No setup, no acks, no resends, less overhead.
TCP fits when every byte matters: web, email, file copies.
UDP fits when late data is useless (voice, video, games) or for tiny query-and-answer exchanges.

cards.title: The three-way handshake
cards.body: TCP opens a connection with three messages. Each side picks a starting sequence number and the other side acknowledges it. Closing uses FIN messages.
cards.code:
client          server
  --- SYN -------->
  <-- SYN, ACK ----
  --- ACK -------->
  connection open

cards.title: Ports pick the program
cards.body: IP gets data to the right host; a port number gets it to the right program. Ports are 16-bit numbers, 0 to 65535. A connection is told apart by four values: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. Servers listen on well-known ports; a client picks a fresh temporary source port for each connection.

cards.title: Port ranges
bullets: 0-1023: well-known (system) ports.
1024-49151: registered ports.
49152-65535: dynamic ports, used by clients.

cards.title: Common ports
cards.code:
HTTP    TCP 80
HTTPS   TCP 443
SMTP    TCP 25   send mail
POP3    TCP 110  fetch mail
SSH     TCP 22
DNS     UDP 53

cards.title: Why IPv6
cards.body: The public IPv4 supply ran out: IANA gave away its last blocks in 2011. NAT and CIDR stretched IPv4, but IPv6 is the long-term fix. Its addresses are 128 bits, about 3.4 x 10**38 of them.

cards.title: Writing an address
cards.body: An IPv6 address is 32 hex digits in eight groups of four, split by colons. The block 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for examples. Python can shorten or expand one:
cards.code:
import ipaddress
a = ipaddress.ip_address(
    '2001:0db8:0070:0000:'
    '0000:0000:0c00:0001')
print(a)  # 2001:db8:70::c00:1
print(a.exploded)  # full form

cards.title: Shortening rules
bullets: In each group, drop leading zeros: 0db8 becomes db8, 0000 becomes 0.
Never drop trailing zeros: 0c00 becomes c00, not c.
Replace one run of two or more all-zero groups with ::, the longest run (the first if tied).
Only one :: per address, or nobody could tell how many zeros each hides.
To expand, pad groups to 4 digits and let :: fill zero groups up to eight.

cards.title: Prefix length
cards.body: IPv6 writes masks only as a prefix length, /0 to /128. LAN subnets are usually /64: the first 64 bits (4 groups) name the subnet and the last 64 name the host. For the subnet prefix, keep the first P bits and set the rest to 0.

cards.title: Same ideas, new parts
bullets: Hosts still need an address and a default router.
Routers still route by longest prefix match.
ICMPv6 replaces ICMP, and Neighbor Discovery (NDP) replaces ARP.
The base header is a fixed 40 bytes.
Dual stack: devices run IPv4 and IPv6 side by side.

cards.title: What current is
cards.body: Current is charge flowing past a point. Charge is counted in coulombs (C) and current in amperes (A). One amp means one coulomb passing every second, so I = Q / t, and the charge moved is Q = I × t.

cards.title: Small units
bullets: 1 mA (milliamp) = 0.001 A
1 µA (microamp) = 0.000001 A
A small indicator LED runs on about 20 mA
Example: 0.2 A for 10 s moves 2 C

cards.title: Which way it flows
cards.body: In a metal wire the charges that move are electrons, and they drift from the battery's negative terminal toward the positive one. Diagrams and formulas use conventional current instead, drawn from + through the circuit back to −. It points the opposite way, but every calculation comes out the same.

cards.title: Counting electrons
cards.body: One electron carries about 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so one coulomb is roughly 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons. Divide the charge by the electron's charge to count them.
cards.code:
e = 1.602e-19      # C each
amps, secs = 0.5, 4
q = amps * secs    # 2.0 C
print(q / e)       # ~1.25e19

cards.title: Slow drift, fast push
cards.body: Each electron drifts very slowly, often well under a millimetre per second. The push travels along the wire at a large fraction of the speed of light, which is why a lamp lights the moment the switch closes.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: A push between points
cards.body: Voltage is the electrical push that drives current, measured in volts (V). It always compares two points. One volt means each coulomb moved between them gains or gives up one joule (1 V = 1 J/C), so energy = V × Q.

cards.title: Ground means 0 V
cards.body: Pick one point, call it ground, and treat it as 0 V. A label like "5 V at node A" means 5 V measured from ground. The voltage between two labelled nodes is the difference of their labels. In battery circuits ground is usually the negative terminal.

cards.title: Stacking batteries
cards.body: Cells joined + to − in series add their voltages. Moving ground to the middle gives a split supply. Cells in parallel keep the same voltage but last longer; only parallel matching, fresh cells.
cards.code:
two 4.5 V batteries in series
ground at the bottom:
  0 V, +4.5 V, +9 V
ground in the middle:
  -4.5 V, 0 V, +4.5 V

cards.title: One wire, one voltage
cards.body: Every point along a plain wire sits at almost the same voltage, so a voltmeter across a wire reads about 0 V. The voltage is used up across the parts that resist current, such as a lamp or a resistor.

cards.title: Earth ground
cards.body: The ground symbol can also mean a real link to the earth. A mains outlet's earth pin connects to a rod in the soil, and metal equipment cases are tied to it, so a fault sends current into the earth instead of through a person.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: Ohm's law
cards.body: Resistance (R) is how strongly a part opposes current, in ohms (Ω). For a resistor the three quantities are linked by V = I × R, which rearranges to I = V / R and R = V / I. Some parts, such as diodes, don't follow this straight-line rule.

cards.title: Worked example
cards.code:
9 V across 360 Ω
I = V / R = 9 / 360
  = 0.025 A = 25 mA
bullets: Convert mA to A before dividing
Volts ÷ kΩ gives mA: 10 V / 2 kΩ = 5 mA

cards.title: Shape and material
cards.body: A wire's resistance is R = ρ × L / A. Doubling the length doubles R; doubling the cross-section area halves it. ρ (resistivity, in Ω·m) belongs to the material: copper is about 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, while glass is above 10¹⁰ Ω·m.

cards.title: Conductors and insulators
bullets: Metals: many free electrons, very low ρ
Insulators (glass, rubber): almost none, huge ρ
Semiconductors (silicon): in between
Heat raises a metal's resistance but lowers a semiconductor's

cards.title: Opens and shorts
cards.body: An open circuit is a break, so no current flows. A short is an accidental path with almost no resistance. The current is then V divided by whatever small resistances are left in the loop, added together (the wire plus the battery's own internal resistance). It can be huge, which is why fuses exist.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: What power is
cards.body: Power is how fast energy is used, in watts (1 W = 1 joule per second). For any part, multiply the voltage across it by the current through it: P = V × I. A 230 V kettle drawing 10 A uses 2,300 W.

cards.title: Power in resistors
cards.body: Put Ohm's law into P = V × I and you get two handy forms: P = I² × R when you know the current, and P = V² / R when you know the voltage. In a resistor all of that power turns into heat.

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
i, r = 0.03, 150.0  # 30 mA
v = i * r           # 4.5 V
print(round(v * i, 3))     # VI
print(round(i**2 * r, 3))  # I²R
print(round(v**2 / r, 3))  # V²/R
# all three print 0.135 (W)

cards.title: Power ratings
bullets: Common resistor ratings: 1/8, 1/4, 1/2 and 1 W
Past its rating a resistor overheats and fails
Rule of thumb: pick at least twice the expected power
Energy = power × time (joules = watts × seconds)

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: In series
cards.body: Parts in series sit one after another on a single path. The same current flows through each, their voltages add up to the supply, and the total resistance is the sum: R = R1 + R2 + …

cards.title: In parallel
cards.body: Parts in parallel all connect across the same two points, so each gets the same voltage. The supply current splits between the branches, and the total resistance falls below the smallest branch: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …

cards.title: Quick rules
bullets: ∥ is short for "in parallel with"
Two in parallel: R1 × R2 / (R1 + R2)
n equal resistors in parallel: R / n
Equal bulbs in series dim; in parallel each gets full voltage

cards.title: Simplify step by step
cards.body: Shrink a network one piece at a time: replace an obvious series or parallel group with its total, redraw, and repeat. Work from the innermost brackets out.

cards.title: In Python

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Two resistors in series across a supply split its voltage in proportion to their sizes. Take the output from the middle: Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2). R2 is the resistor between the output and ground; R1 goes up to the supply.

cards.title: Worked example
cards.code:
Vin = 12 V
R1 = 2 kΩ (top)
R2 = 1 kΩ (to ground)
Vout = 12 × 1 / (2 + 1)
     = 4 V

cards.title: Picking R1
cards.body: To get a chosen output, fix R2 and rearrange: R1 = R2 × (Vin − Vout) / Vout. For 12 V down to 3.3 V with R2 = 3.3 kΩ: R1 = 3.3 kΩ × 8.7 / 3.3 = 8.7 kΩ.

cards.title: Loads pull it down
cards.body: A load across the output sits in parallel with R2. That lowers the bottom resistance, so Vout drops. Allow for the load's current when choosing R1, or use a voltage regulator for loads that change.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: Current law
cards.body: At any junction, the current flowing in equals the current flowing out. Charge can't pile up or vanish, so the branches must balance.
cards.code:
junction: 40 mA in
out: 15 mA, 10 mA and I3
I3 = 40 - 15 - 10 = 15 mA

cards.title: Voltage law
cards.body: Go around any closed loop and the voltage rises and drops add to zero. In a single loop, the drops across the parts add up to the source voltage. It is energy bookkeeping: a charge back where it started has gained nothing.
cards.code:
9 V supply, two resistors
R1 drops 3.5 V
R2 drops 9 - 3.5 = 5.5 V

cards.title: Current divider
cards.body: When a current splits between two parallel resistors, more goes through the smaller one: I1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2). By the current law, the other branch carries the rest, I − I1.

cards.title: Using them
cards.body: For a tricky network, write a current-law equation at each junction and a voltage-law equation around each loop, then solve them together. The laws hold for any parts, including diodes and transistors, not just resistors.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: DC and AC
cards.body: Direct current (DC) flows one way from a steady source like a battery. Alternating current (AC) keeps reversing direction, and its voltage swings positive and negative, usually as a smooth sine wave. Mains power is AC, partly because transformers can raise or lower AC voltage efficiently.

cards.title: Frequency and period
cards.body: Frequency f is the number of full cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). The period T is the time one cycle takes, so T = 1 / f and f = 1 / T.
bullets: 1 kHz gives T = 1 ms
A 1 µs period means 1 MHz
US mains: 120 V at 60 Hz; much of the world: 220–240 V at 50 Hz

cards.title: Peak and peak-to-peak
cards.body: The peak (Vp) is the highest point of the wave, measured from 0 V. Peak-to-peak (Vpp) runs from the lowest point to the highest, so for a sine Vpp = 2 × Vp.

cards.title: RMS values
cards.body: A sine averages to zero, so it is rated by RMS (root mean square: square, average, square root). RMS is the DC voltage that would heat a resistor just as much. For a sine, Vrms = Vp / √2 ≈ 0.707 × Vp, and Vp ≈ 1.414 × Vrms. Mains ratings like 120 V are RMS.

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
import math
vrms = 230
vp = vrms * math.sqrt(2)
print(round(vp, 1))      # 325.3
print(round(2 * vp, 1))  # 650.5

cards.title: AC power in resistors
cards.body: With RMS values, Ohm's law and the power formulas work on a plain resistor just as they do for DC: Irms = Vrms / R, and P = Vrms² / R gives the average power. Using the peak voltage instead would double the answer.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: Wire gauge
cards.body: Wire thickness is given as a gauge number (AWG in the US). The scale runs backwards: a smaller number means a thicker wire. Thicker wire has less resistance and safely carries more current; push too much through a thin wire and it heats up and can melt.

cards.title: Solid or stranded
bullets: Solid core: one wire; pushes neatly into breadboards but snaps after much bending
Stranded: many thin strands; flexible, good for cables that move
Magnet wire: varnish-coated, for winding coils

cards.title: Poles and throws
cards.body: Switches are named by poles and throws. A pole is one separate circuit the switch controls; a throw is each contact a pole can connect to. S means single (1) and D means double (2), so a DPDT switch works two circuits at once, each choosing between two contacts.
cards.code:
SPST: 1 pole, 1 throw
SPDT: 1 pole, 2 throws
DPST: 2 poles, 1 throw
DPDT: 2 poles, 2 throws

cards.title: Push buttons
cards.body: Momentary switches spring back when you let go. A normally open (NO) button connects only while it is pressed; a normally closed (NC) one breaks the circuit only while pressed. Some toggle switches also have a center-off position.

cards.title: Special switches
bullets: Reed switch: two thin contacts in glass that close near a magnet (door alarms)
DIP switch: a row of tiny switches that fits a chip socket
Rotary switch: one pole, many throws, e.g. SP8T

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: What a relay is
cards.body: A relay is a switch worked by electricity. Current through its coil makes an electromagnet that pulls a spring-loaded contact across. A small, low-voltage control circuit can then switch a separate, bigger circuit, and the two stay electrically apart.

cards.title: Kinds of relay
bullets: Mechanical: amps of current, switches in about 10–100 ms
Reed: lighter loads, faster (about 0.2–2 ms)
Solid-state: no moving parts, very fast
Contacts are named like switches: SPDT, NO, NC
Coils are rated for a voltage, such as 5, 12 or 24 V DC

cards.title: The flyback diode
cards.body: A relay coil is an inductor, and it fights any sudden change in current. Switch it off and it can kick out a spike of hundreds of volts, enough to destroy the transistor driving it. A diode across the coil, facing so it blocks the normal supply, gives that current a safe loop to die away in.

cards.title: Fuses and breakers
cards.body: A fuse is a thin metal link that melts when the current goes past its rating, opening the circuit; it must then be replaced. A circuit breaker trips instead and can be reset. Both protect wiring and parts from shorts and overloads.

cards.title: Choosing a fuse
bullets: Fast-blow: opens on a brief surge; for sensitive electronics
Slow-blow (time-lag): rides out turn-on surges from motors
Rating: about 50% above the normal current
On mains, put it in the hot (live) wire, before the device

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: Color digits
cards.body: Small through-hole resistors are marked with colored bands. Each color stands for a digit:
cards.code:
black  0    green  5
brown  1    blue   6
red    2    violet 7
orange 3    gray   8
yellow 4    white  9

cards.title: Reading four bands
cards.body: Start from the end away from the gold or silver band. Bands 1 and 2 are digits, band 3 is the multiplier (how many zeros to add, a power of ten), and band 4 is the tolerance.
cards.code:
green blue red  gold
5     6    ×100 ±5%
= 5,600 Ω = 5.6 kΩ

cards.title: Tolerance and five bands
bullets: Gold ±5%, silver ±10%, no band ±20%
Brown ±1%, red ±2% (precision parts)
Gold or silver as band 3 multiplies by 0.1 or 0.01
Five bands: three digits, then multiplier, then tolerance

cards.title: What tolerance means
cards.body: Tolerance is how far the real value may be from the printed one. A 470 Ω ±5% part can be anywhere from 446.5 Ω to 493.5 Ω: 5% of 470 is 23.5 Ω either way. For most hobby circuits ±5% is fine.

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
C = ["black", "brown", "red",
     "orange", "yellow", "green",
     "blue", "violet", "gray",
     "white"]

def ohms(b1, b2, b3):
    i = C.index
    n = 10 * i(b1) + i(b2)
    return n * 10 ** i(b3)

print(ohms("green", "blue", "red"))
# 5600

cards.title: Storing charge
cards.body: A capacitor is two conducting plates with an insulator between them. Put a voltage across it and it stores charge: Q = C × V. Capacitance C is in farads (F); real parts run from a few pF to tens of thousands of µF.

cards.title: DC blocked, AC passed
cards.body: Once charged, a capacitor lets no steady DC through. Changing signals do pass, and more easily at higher frequency: its reactance is Xc = 1 / (2πfC) ohms. In series it blocks DC between stages; from a supply line to ground it drains away noise.

cards.title: Combining capacitors
bullets: Parallel: capacitances add, C = C1 + C2
Series: 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2, smaller than either
These are the opposite of the resistor rules
A parallel group is limited by its lowest voltage rating

cards.title: RC time constant
cards.body: Charging through a resistor takes time. The time constant is τ = R × C (ohms × farads = seconds). From 0 V the voltage is V = Vs × (1 − e^(−t/τ)): 63.2% of the supply after one τ, about full after five. Discharging, V = V0 × e^(−t/τ).
cards.code:
import math
for n in range(1, 6):
    pct = 100 * (1 - math.exp(-n))
    print(n, round(pct, 1))
# 63.2 86.5 95.0 98.2 99.3

cards.title: Electrolytics have polarity
cards.body: Electrolytic capacitors pack large values into small cans but are polarized: the + lead must stay more positive than the − lead. Reverse them, or go past their voltage rating, and they can overheat, leak or burst. Ceramic capacitors hold small values and work either way round.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: What an inductor is
cards.body: An inductor is a coil of wire, often wound on an iron or ferrite core. It resists any change in the current through it: the faster the current changes, the bigger the voltage it develops (V = L × ΔI / Δt). Inductance L is measured in henrys (H).

cards.title: AC versus DC
cards.body: Steady DC passes, meeting only the wire's small resistance. AC is opposed more as frequency rises: the reactance is XL = 2πfL ohms, so it grows in step with the frequency. That is the opposite of a capacitor, and it is why coils work as chokes against high-frequency noise.

cards.title: Combining coils
bullets: Series: inductances add
Parallel: 1/L = 1/L1 + 1/L2
Both hold when the coils don't share magnetic field
Cutting a coil's current suddenly causes a voltage spike

cards.title: How transformers work
cards.body: A transformer is two coils on one iron core. AC in the primary makes a changing magnetic field that induces a voltage in the secondary, in the ratio of the turns: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np. Steady DC makes no changing field, so a transformer can't convert it.

cards.title: Current trades off
cards.body: An ideal transformer passes on all its power, so Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. Step the voltage down and the current steps up by the same ratio: Is / Ip = Np / Ns. Real ones waste some power as heat.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: A one-way valve
cards.body: A diode lets current through in one direction only. It has an anode (the p side) and a cathode (the n side, marked with a band). When the anode is more positive than the cathode it is forward-biased and conducts; reversed, it blocks.

cards.title: Forward voltage
bullets: Silicon: about 0.6–0.7 V before it conducts
Schottky: about 0.4 V, and faster
Germanium: about 0.2–0.3 V
Diodes in series add their drops
Limits: max forward current and peak reverse voltage (PIV)

cards.title: AC to DC
cards.body: A rectifier turns AC into DC. One diode (half-wave) passes only the positive halves, giving pulsing DC. A bridge of four diodes uses both halves, but the current always crosses two diodes, so the output peak is two drops below the input peak. A capacitor after it smooths the ripple.

cards.title: Bridge example
cards.code:
transformer gives 6 V RMS
peak = 6 × 1.414 ≈ 8.5 V
bridge loses 2 × 0.7 = 1.4 V
output peak ≈ 7.1 V

cards.title: Other diode jobs
bullets: Series diode: blocks a battery put in backwards
Flyback diode: soaks up a coil's switch-off spike
Zener diode: conducts in reverse at a set voltage, for simple regulators

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 4

cards.title: Light from a diode
cards.body: An LED is a diode built to give off light when forward-biased. Like any diode it conducts one way only: the anode (usually the longer lead) goes toward +, the cathode (shorter lead, flat edge on the rim) toward −. Brightness follows the current.

cards.title: Forward voltage
bullets: Red: about 1.7–2 V
Yellow and green: about 2–2.1 V
White and most blue: about 3.4–3.6 V
Typical current 10–30 mA; assume 20 mA if unsure

cards.title: The series resistor
cards.body: An LED hardly limits its own current: a little above its forward voltage the current shoots up and burns it out. So add a resistor in series: R = (Vsupply − Vled) / I, then round up to the next standard value.
cards.code:
12 V supply, LED drops 3.4 V
want 20 mA
R = (12 - 3.4) / 0.02
  = 430 Ω

cards.title: Several LEDs
cards.body: LEDs in series can share one resistor: subtract all their forward voltages from the supply first. Don't run LEDs in parallel from a single resistor; whichever warms up takes more of the current. Give each its own resistor.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 5

cards.title: Small controls big
cards.body: A transistor uses a small signal on one lead to control a larger current through the other two, like a hand on a tap. It can act as an electronic switch or as an amplifier. The two big families are bipolar transistors (BJTs) and field-effect transistors (FETs).

cards.title: NPN basics
cards.body: An NPN bipolar transistor has a base, a collector and an emitter. It turns on when current flows into the base, which sits about 0.6–0.7 V above the emitter. A PNP works the same way with every polarity flipped.

cards.title: Current gain
cards.body: In its active region a small base current controls a bigger collector current: Ic = β × Ib. The gain β (also written hFE) varies from part to part, typically 10 to 500. Both currents leave through the emitter, so Ie = Ib + Ic.

cards.title: Three regions
bullets: Cutoff: no base current, collector-emitter acts like an open switch
Active: Ic follows β × Ib, so small changes are made bigger
Saturation: driven fully on, acts like a closed switch

cards.title: As a switch
cards.body: To switch a load, find the base current it needs, Ib = Ic / β, and size the base resistor from the control voltage: Rb = (Vin − 0.7) / Ib. Pick a somewhat smaller resistor so it is surely saturated.

cards.title: Field-effect transistors (MOSFETs)
cards.body: A MOSFET's gate is insulated, so it draws almost no current; voltage alone controls it. A common n-channel enhancement MOSFET is off with 0 V on its gate and turns on once the gate is a few volts above the source. FETs are the workhorse of modern chips.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 4

cards.title: Two kinds of signal
cards.body: An analog signal can take any value in a range, like a thermometer voltage drifting smoothly from 0.31 V to 0.47 V. A digital signal uses just two levels, HIGH and LOW, so each wire carries one bit. Digital circuits can store bits and make logical decisions, which plain analog circuits can't.

cards.title: Logic levels
bullets: Usually HIGH = 1 = true and LOW = 0 = false (positive true logic)
Negative true logic swaps them: LOW means true
In a 5 V system, near 5 V counts as HIGH and near 0 V as LOW
Each logic family sets its own valid voltage bands; a voltage between them is not a valid level

cards.title: The clock
cards.body: Most digital systems keep time with a clock signal. It flips between HIGH and LOW over and over, f times per second. One full cycle takes T = 1/f seconds, and circuits do their work when it switches.

cards.title: Serial or parallel
cards.body: Serial sends a word down one data wire, one bit per clock period, so n bits take n periods: O(n) time. Parallel gives every bit its own wire and moves the whole word in one period: faster, but it needs n wires.
cards.code:
12-bit word, T = 100 ns
serial:   12 x 100 = 1200 ns
parallel:  1 x 100 =  100 ns

cards.title: Logic families
bullets: CMOS: built from MOSFETs, low power; almost all logic today
TTL: older family of bipolar transistors, made for 5 V
Fanout: how many same-family inputs one output can drive
Propagation delay: time from an input change to the output change, in nanoseconds

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Place values
cards.body: Binary uses only 0 and 1. Each place is worth twice the place on its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. The leftmost bit is the most significant bit (MSB), the rightmost the least significant (LSB). To read a number, add the values under every 1.

cards.title: Decimal to binary
cards.body: Divide by 2 again and again and keep each remainder. The first remainder is the LSB and the last one is the MSB, so read them from the bottom up.

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: divmod(n, 2) gives the whole quotient n // 2 and the remainder n % 2. One loop pass per bit: O(log n) time, and O(log n) space for the digits.

cards.title: Hexadecimal (base 16)
cards.body: Hex is base 16: digits 0 to 9, then A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so split binary into groups of 4 from the right (pad with 0s on the left) and swap each group for its digit. Octal does the same with groups of 3.

cards.title: Handy facts
bullets: 8 bits = 2 hex digits; 32 bits = 8 hex digits
Decimal to hex: divide by 16 and keep the remainders, like with 2
Python: hex(235) gives '0xeb', int('EB', 16) gives 235

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Binary-coded decimal
cards.body: BCD stores each decimal digit in its own 4-bit group. It suits digit displays like clocks and meters. Only 0000 to 1001 (0 to 9) are valid groups; 1010 to 1111 never appear.

cards.title: BCD is not binary
cards.body: Converting digit by digit is not the same as converting the whole number. 25 in BCD is 0010 0101, but 25 in plain binary is 0001 1001. BCD needs more bits for the same value.

cards.title: Two's complement
cards.body: Circuits store negatives in two's complement. Positives are plain binary. For a negative, write the positive value, flip every bit (the one's complement), then add 1. The top bit then shows the sign: 1 means negative. 8 bits hold -128 to +127. Sign-magnitude, which only sets the top bit, is rarely used for math.

cards.title: Adding in binary
cards.body: Add columns from the right: 0+1 = 1, 1+1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1), 1+1+1 = 11 (write 1, carry 1). With two's complement, subtracting is adding the negative; drop any carry out of the top bit. n-bit numbers take n column steps: O(n).

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: What a gate does
cards.body: A logic gate takes one or more input bits and gives one output bit. A truth table lists the output for every input combination. n inputs give 2ⁿ rows, so writing out a full table takes O(2ⁿ) time.

cards.title: The basic gates
bullets: NOT: flips its one input
AND: 1 only if every input is 1
OR: 1 if at least one input is 1
XOR: 1 if the two inputs differ
NAND, NOR, XNOR: AND, OR, XOR with the output flipped

cards.title: More inputs
cards.body: AND, OR, NAND and NOR also come with 3, 4 or 8 inputs. A 4-input AND gives 1 in only one of its 16 rows (all 1s), and a 4-input OR gives 0 in only one row (all 0s). NAND and NOR flip those outputs, so their counts swap.

cards.title: Gates in Python
cards.body: On the bits 0 and 1, Python's & is AND, | is OR and ^ is XOR. 1 - x flips a bit.
cards.code:
a, b = 1, 0
print(a & b)        # AND  0
print(a | b)        # OR   1
print(a ^ b)        # XOR  1
print(1 - a)        # NOT  0
print(1 - (a & b))  # NAND 1
print(int(a == b))  # XNOR 0

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Writing logic
bullets: A·B (or AB) means A AND B
A + B means A OR B, so 1 + 1 = 1
A' means NOT A (books draw a bar over A)
A ⊕ B means A XOR B

cards.title: Handy identities
cards.code:
A + 0 = A      A · 1 = A
A + 1 = 1      A · 0 = 0
A + A = A      A · A = A
A + A' = 1     A · A' = 0
A'' = A
A + A·B = A   (absorption)
A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C

cards.title: Simplifying an expression
cards.body: Fewer terms mean fewer gates. Factor out what the terms share, then apply the identities. Here Y' is in both terms:

cards.title: De Morgan's laws
cards.body: To split a bar over a group, flip each variable and swap AND with OR. So a NAND acts like an OR gate whose inputs are inverted first, and a NOR like an AND with inverted inputs. Swapping the gate and moving the bubbles this way is called bubble pushing.

cards.title: Check every row
cards.body: Two expressions are equal if they agree on every row. With n variables that is 2ⁿ rows: O(2ⁿ) time.
cards.code:
rows = [(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)]
for a, b in rows:
    assert 1-(a|b) == (1-a)&(1-b)
print('De Morgan holds')

cards.title: Universal gates
cards.body: NAND alone can build every other gate, and so can NOR. Tie a NAND's inputs together and it becomes NOT; add that NOT after a NAND and you get AND. Simplified designs usually end up as a sum of products (ORed AND terms, like A·B + C) or a product of sums; Karnaugh maps help find the simplest one.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: No memory
cards.body: In combinational logic the output depends only on the inputs right now. Change an input and the output follows after a few nanoseconds of delay. Common blocks come ready-made as chips.

cards.title: Pick and route
bullets: Multiplexer (mux): n select lines choose one of 2ⁿ inputs and pass it to the one output
Demultiplexer: sends one input to one of 2ⁿ outputs
Decoder: an n-bit code turns on exactly one of 2ⁿ output lines
Encoder: the reverse; the one active input becomes its binary code. A priority encoder picks the highest if several are active

cards.title: Active-low outputs
cards.body: Many decoders mark the chosen line by pulling it LOW while every other line stays HIGH. A bubble on the pin, or a bar over its name, shows this. Example: a 2-to-4 decoder with active-low outputs that gets the code 10 makes Y2 LOW and keeps Y0, Y1 and Y3 HIGH.

cards.title: Half and full adders
cards.body: A half adder adds two bits: sum = A XOR B, carry = A AND B. A full adder also takes a carry in. It is two half adders (A with B, then that sum with the carry in) plus an OR that merges their two carries.

cards.title: Half adder in Python
cards.code:
def half_add(a, b):
    return a ^ b, a & b

print(half_add(1, 1))  # (0, 1)
print(half_add(1, 0))  # (1, 0)

cards.title: Ripple-carry adder
cards.body: Chain n full adders, each carry out feeding the next carry in, to add two n-bit numbers. The top stage must wait for the carry to ripple through every stage, so the worst-case delay is n stage delays: O(n) time, using O(n) gates.
cards.code:
8 stages, 5 ns per carry
worst case: 8 x 5 = 40 ns

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Logic with memory
cards.body: Sequential logic stores bits, so its output depends on past inputs as well as present ones. The basic one-bit store is a latch or flip-flop. A clock usually decides when it takes in new data.

cards.title: SR latch
cards.body: Two cross-coupled NOR gates with inputs S (set) and R (reset). With both at 0 the latch remembers. S = R = 1 forces both outputs to 0, and the state after release is a race, so it is avoided. A NAND latch has active-low inputs: its hold state is 1 1.
cards.code:
S R   Q next
0 0   Q   (hold)
1 0   1   (set)
0 1   0   (reset)
1 1   not allowed

cards.title: Level vs edge
cards.body: A level-triggered (gated) latch follows its inputs the whole time its clock or enable is HIGH. An edge-triggered flip-flop looks at its inputs only at the instant the clock rises (or falls) and ignores changes at any other time.

cards.title: D flip-flop
cards.body: A D flip-flop feeds D to S and an inverted copy to R, so S = R = 1 can't happen. At each active clock edge Q takes the value of D; between edges Q holds. D must be steady for a short setup time before the edge, or Q may be wrong.

cards.title: JK flip-flop
cards.body: JK works like SR, but J = K = 1 toggles instead of being forbidden: Q flips on every active edge.
cards.code:
J K   Q after the edge
0 0   Q    (hold)
1 0   1    (set)
0 1   0    (reset)
1 1   Q'   (toggle)

cards.title: Tracing a JK
cards.code:
Q starts at 1
edge  J K   Q after
 1    0 1   0  reset
 2    1 1   1  toggle
 3    0 0   1  hold
 4    1 1   0  toggle

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Counting with toggles
cards.body: A flip-flop in toggle mode flips once per clock edge, so its output runs at half the clock frequency. Chain n of them, each clocked by the one before, and you get a ripple counter: it counts 0 to 2ⁿ - 1 (MOD-2ⁿ) and divides the clock by 2ⁿ at its last output.

cards.title: Sizing a counter
cards.code:
flip-flops  states  counts to
 1           2        1
 3           8        7
 4          16       15
10        1024     1023

100 kHz in, 4 stages:
100 / 16 = 6.25 kHz out

cards.title: Ripple vs synchronous
cards.body: In a ripple counter each stage waits for the one before, so delays add up: 4 stages of 25 ns settle 100 ns after the edge, O(n) for n stages. A synchronous counter clocks every flip-flop from one shared clock and uses gates to pick which ones toggle, so all outputs change together.

cards.title: Shift registers
cards.body: A row of D flip-flops where each Q feeds the next D. On each clock edge every bit moves one place, so loading n bits serially takes n clocks.
bullets: Serial-in, serial-out: delays a bit stream
Serial-in, parallel-out: collects bits into a word
Parallel-in, serial-out: sends a word one bit per clock

cards.title: Ring and Johnson
cards.body: Feed the last output back to the first input and a single 1 goes round and round: a ring counter of n flip-flops has n states. Feed back the inverted last output instead and you get a Johnson counter with 2n states.
cards.code:
3-bit Johnson counter:
000 100 110 111 011 001
then back to 000 (6 states)

cards.title: Shifting in Python
cards.body: A list can model a register. Each shift copies the list: O(n) time and space per clock in Python, though the hardware moves all bits at once.
cards.code:
reg = [0, 0, 0]
for bit in [1, 1, 0]:
    reg = reg[1:] + [bit]  # left
    print(reg)

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Tables and queries
cards.body: A table stores rows, and every row has the same named columns. A SELECT query describes the rows and columns you want; the database works out how to fetch them. Keywords are not case-sensitive, and a statement ends with a semicolon. The examples use this songs table:
cards.code:
id title artist year plays
1  Glow  1      2019 420
2  Drift 1      2021 150
3  Tide  2      1998 900
4  Spark 2      2022 NULL
5  Echo  NULL   2005 60

cards.title: Pick and filter
cards.code:
SELECT title, plays
FROM songs
WHERE year >= 2000
  AND plays > 100;
-- Glow 420, Drift 150
cards.body: SELECT lists the columns (* means all), FROM names the table, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. AND binds tighter than OR, so use parentheses when you mix them.

cards.title: Handy filters
bullets: IN (1, 3): matches any value in the list.
BETWEEN 2019 AND 2021: a range that includes both ends.
LIKE 'D%': % stands for any run of characters, _ for exactly one. In SQLite, LIKE ignores case for plain letters.
DISTINCT: drops duplicate rows from the result.

cards.title: Sorting and limits
cards.code:
SELECT title, year
FROM songs
ORDER BY year DESC
LIMIT 2;
-- Spark 2022, Drift 2021
cards.body: ORDER BY sorts ascending unless you add DESC; extra columns break ties. LIMIT n keeps the first n rows (SQL Server uses TOP instead). Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed.

cards.title: Clause order, cost
cards.body: Write clauses in this order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT. With no index, WHERE has to scan every row: O(n) time. ORDER BY needs a sort, O(n log n) time and O(n) space, unless an index already keeps that order.

cards.title: Unknown, not zero
cards.body: NULL marks a missing or unknown value. It is not 0 and not the empty string ''. Comparing anything with NULL, even NULL = NULL, gives NULL (unknown), and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. So unknown rows quietly drop out.

cards.title: Test with IS
cards.body: Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL; = NULL never matches.

cards.title: Three-valued logic
bullets: TRUE AND NULL is NULL; FALSE AND NULL is FALSE.
TRUE OR NULL is TRUE; FALSE OR NULL is NULL.
NOT NULL is still NULL.
So WHERE x <> 5 also skips rows where x is NULL.

cards.title: Filling the gaps
cards.body: COALESCE(a, b, ...) returns its first argument that is not NULL. SQLite also has IFNULL(a, b) for two arguments. Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: 5 + NULL is NULL.
cards.code:
SELECT title,
  COALESCE(plays, 0)
FROM songs;
-- Spark shows 0

cards.title: Aggregate functions
cards.code:
SELECT COUNT(*),      -- 5
       COUNT(plays),  -- 4
       SUM(plays),    -- 1530
       AVG(plays)     -- 382.5
FROM songs;
cards.body: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip NULLs, so AVG divides by 4 here, not 5.

cards.title: Grouping rows
cards.body: GROUP BY puts rows with the same value into one group and returns one row per group. Each selected column should be grouped or wrapped in an aggregate; SQLite is looser and lets other columns through, but their values come from just one row of the group.

cards.title: WHERE versus HAVING
cards.code:
SELECT artist_id,
       COUNT(*) AS n
FROM songs
WHERE year > 2000
GROUP BY artist_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
-- artist 1, n = 2
cards.body: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after the aggregates exist, so COUNT(*) belongs in HAVING; in WHERE it is an error.

cards.title: Run order, cost
cards.body: The database runs FROM, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY and LIMIT. Grouping by sorting costs O(n log n) time; grouping with a hash table costs O(n) average time and O(g) space for g groups.

cards.title: Why join
cards.body: Data is split over tables that point at each other with keys: songs.artist_id holds an id from artists. A join puts matching rows side by side, and ON gives the matching rule. Short aliases (FROM songs AS s) keep column names clear: s.title. Artists here: 1 Nova, 2 Lumen, 3 Quill.

cards.title: INNER JOIN
cards.code:
SELECT s.title, a.name
FROM songs AS s
JOIN artists AS a
  ON a.id = s.artist_id;
-- 4 rows; Echo has no
-- artist, so it is left out
cards.body: Plain JOIN means INNER JOIN: only rows with a match on both sides.

cards.title: LEFT JOIN
cards.code:
SELECT a.name, s.title
FROM artists AS a
LEFT JOIN songs AS s
  ON s.artist_id = a.id;
-- 5 rows: Nova 2, Lumen 2,
-- Quill once, title NULL
cards.body: Every row of the left table stays. Where nothing matches, the right side's columns are NULL. Add WHERE s.id IS NULL to keep only the rows with no match: Quill.

cards.title: What joins cost
cards.body: A nested-loop join with no index compares every pair: O(n·m) time for tables of n and m rows. With an index on the inner table's join column it is about O(n log m). A join with no matching rule (CROSS JOIN) returns all n·m pairs.

cards.title: Adding rows
cards.body: List the columns, then VALUES with one value per column. Columns you leave out get their default, or NULL. You can add several rows at once: VALUES (...), (...).

cards.title: Changing rows
cards.body: SET gives the new values and WHERE picks the rows. A row whose plays is NULL stays NULL, since NULL + 10 is NULL.

cards.title: Removing rows
cards.code:
DELETE FROM songs
WHERE year < 2000;
cards.body: DELETE removes rows but keeps the table; DROP TABLE removes the table itself.

cards.title: Mind the WHERE
bullets: UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE hits every row.
Run the WHERE in a SELECT first to see which rows match.
Wrap risky changes in BEGIN ... COMMIT, or ROLLBACK to undo.
Cost: finding rows is O(n) without an index, and each change also updates every index on the table.

cards.title: Primary keys
cards.body: A primary key is a column, or set of columns, whose value picks out exactly one row. The database rejects a duplicate. In SQLite an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column fills itself in with the next number when you leave it out of an INSERT.

cards.title: Foreign keys
cards.body: A foreign key column holds a key from another table, for example songs.artist_id pointing at artists.id. With checks on, the database refuses a child row whose parent doesn't exist, and by default refuses to delete a parent that rows still point at. A NULL foreign key is allowed.

cards.title: Turn checks on
cards.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=1")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE a(id INTEGER
  PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE b(a_id INTEGER
  REFERENCES a(id));""")
try:
    db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO b VALUES (99)")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print(e)  # FOREIGN KEY ...
cards.body: SQLite leaves foreign key checks off unless each connection runs PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON (or = 1), outside a transaction.

cards.title: Other constraints
bullets: NOT NULL: the column must have a value.
UNIQUE: no two rows share the value.
CHECK (plays >= 0): every row must pass the test.
DEFAULT 0: the value used when none is given.

cards.title: A sorted lookup
cards.body: An index is a separate, sorted copy of one or more columns, with a pointer to each row, like the index at the back of a book. SQLite stores it as a B-tree. UNIQUE and primary key columns are indexed for you (an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the table's own sort key).
cards.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_songs_year
ON songs(year);

cards.title: Why it is faster
cards.body: Without an index, finding rows means a full table scan: O(n). With one, the database searches the tree in O(log n) and then fetches the matching rows. Range filters, joins and ORDER BY on that column can use it too. An index on (a, b) helps queries on a, or a and b, but usually not on b alone.

cards.title: See the plan
cards.code:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM songs
WHERE year = 2021;
-- no index: SCAN songs
-- with it:  SEARCH songs
--   USING INDEX idx_songs_year
cards.body: SCAN means every row is read; SEARCH means an index narrows it down.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Extra storage: O(n) space per index.
Slower writes: each INSERT, DELETE, or UPDATE of an indexed column also updates the index, O(log n) per index.
A plain index allows duplicates; only UNIQUE refuses them.
Index columns you often search, join or sort on, not every column.

cards.title: Each fact once
cards.body: Normalizing means splitting tables so each fact is stored in one place. Here Ana's town is copied into every order she makes:
cards.code:
orders
id name town  item
1  Ana  Leeds pen
2  Ana  Leeds ink
3  Ben  York  pad

cards.title: Three anomalies
bullets: Update: Ana moves, you fix one row and miss the other.
Insert: you can't record a new customer until they order.
Delete: removing Ben's only order also loses his town.

cards.title: The first three forms
bullets: 1NF: each cell holds a single value (no 'pen,ink' lists), and a key identifies each row.
2NF: 1NF, and every non-key column depends on the whole key, not part of a two-column key.
3NF: 2NF, and no non-key column depends on another non-key column.

cards.title: The fix and trade-off
cards.body: Split the example into customers(id, name, town) and orders(id, customer_id, item). Now the town lives in one row. The price is more joins when you read; some systems copy data back on purpose (denormalize) to make reads faster.
